audits.title: Fresh meat, meat products and wild game establishments and residue monitoring

recommendations.text: Take urgent action to review the list of approved/pre-listed establishments (slaughterhouses, meat processing, dairy and wild game plants) in order to assure their compliance with the Community requirements. The revised lists should be submitted to the Commission within two months of receiving this report.

Take urgent action to rectify the plant deficiencies found during the mission. A report of the findings, indicating the actions that have or will be taken, should be submitted to the Commission within two months of receiving this report;

Take urgent action to ensure a uniform level of veterinary supervision and implementation of the Community requirements at all Romanian plants currently on the list. A report should be submitted to the Commission, detailing the action taken to improve a) the management of the National Veterinary Health Agency Service at the central level, and b) the co-ordination between the central and local levels;
Take urgent action to ensure that the Council Directive 93/119/EC provisions on the protection of animals at the time of slaughter and killing are followed;
Urgently inform the Commission about the tests carried out with live FMD virus in a Romanian institute (on behalf of Belgium). 10

Establish uniform incubation criteria (temperature and time) for all establishments. The following measurements for double seam check should be made (as a minimum): % overlap, free space, wrinkling rate and internal droop. 7.2. To the European Commission: 7.2.1. Urgently consider the removal of one slaughterhouse from the list (see 5.2.2. & 5.2.3.). 7.2.2. Consider the withdrawal of the "prelisting" arrangement used by the Romanian authorities as laid down in Council Decision 95/408 and revision of the fresh meat list if the information requested and satisfactory guarantees are not forthcoming. 7.2.3. Carry out a further veterinary mission to Romania when the Commission Services are in receipt of a) a revised list of the plants (slaughterhouses, meat processing, dairy and wild game plants) approved by the Romanian Competent Authority for export to the EU (see 7.1.1.) and b) adequate guarantees that the recommendations (7.1.2.-7.1.5.) are being implemented. 11

audits.title: Fishery products (Residues)

recommendations.text: DWLRQDO 5HVLGXH 0RQLWRULQJ 3ODQ The Hygiene and Public Health Institute as part of the CCA prepares an annual residue-monitoring plan for approval by the CCA. After approval in the "Strategic Surveillance Program", a defined number of samples will be taken by officials at local level under surveillance of the district veterinary directorates. The results are collected by the Hygiene and Public Health Institute for presentation to the CCA. The National Residue Monitoring Plan for 2000 has been transmitted in April 2000 and covers all animal species laid down in Directive 95/23/EC, aquaculture-products, eggs, milk and honey. However, it does not comply with the related EU legislation due to the following deficiencies: - No general information under Art. 7 of Dir. 96/23/EC is given; Information on production in the year 1998 is used for the plan 2000; - Screening of thyrostats is done the basis of thyroid gland weight only; - Iasi laboratory is not performing the control of melengestrol acetate in fat as indicated in the plan; - The list of -agonists screened for is too restricted (only Clenbuterol); - Limits of detection of analytical methods used for the control of group A6 substances are too high. Moreover, methods used for confirmation of dimetridazole (spectrophotometer) and nitrofurans (HPTLC) are not specific enough; - The plan objectives are generally fulfilled. Nevertheless, for some compounds, goals were not reached, e.g. for thyrostats in sheep, goats and horses, for -agonists in sheep and for nitrofurans in slaughtered veal calves, young bovines and cows, sheep, goats and horses; - Some districts do not spread their sampling evenly over the year, e.g. Tulcea for which 72 samples were planned for the year 2000, has not taken any sample at the end of the third trimester. The same observations hold true for Vaslui and Brason districts. 4 6DPSOLQJ 3URFHGXUH 5.1.4.1. General Remark Written detailed instructions on the sampling procedure were not given. The necessary information was only transmitted verbally or in a more general way by the "Strategic Surveillance Program", which resulted in different way of taking samples and different material in the districts visited. Particularly the covering administrative documentation was not uniform even though all necessary information could be found. Since sampling is done only by official veterinary personnel it was done professionally in all places visited. The boxes used were suitable for the transport of samples from the stable/slaughterhouse to the concerned laboratory. However, sealing was not always adequate in order to prevent manipulations by any third party. The transport by employees of the veterinary services cannot give sufficient guarantees to prevent manipulation of any third party. The principle of "target sampling" has not been taken into account; samples were always taken "at random". 5.1.4.2. Live Animals The samples were taken in a professional manner with adequate material. However, non-disposable material was used which could not exclude cross contamination (material used for residue samples for chemical analyses need not to be sterile). 5.1.4.3. Abattoirs Samples were taken in a professional manner and with suitable material. When weighing the samples to prepare the right amount of matrix no measures were taken to exclude cross contamination between the different matrixes. The refrigerator in the slaughterhouse used for intermediate storage of official samples was not temperature recorded but the samples were under official control by key-locked doors. &RQWURO RI 'LVWULEXWLRQ DQG 8VH RI 9HWHULQDU\ 'UXJV Based on Ministerial order No.101/1999, the Institute of State Control of Veterinary Biologicals and Medicaments as part of the SVA organises the approval and registration of veterinary drugs. Registered drugs are published in the official journal. Only registered drugs can have a marketing authorisation. However, the national law does not require a registration number marked on each veterinary drug (e.g., on the label or packaging material). The Institute is responsible for the supervision of manufacturers and whole- sellers while the surveillance of local pharmacies, veterinary surgeons and farms is done by the district veterinary services. 5 During the supervision visits all findings are recorded in a protocol-sheet. One copy of these protocols will remain with the establishment visited, the other is kept by the visiting service. The following deficiencies were encountered during visits to a wholesaler, a pharmacy, a veterinary surgery and farms: - Leaflets in the Romanian language are not available at local level. Only the visited important wholesaler/retailer could provide instructions in the local language. - Insufficient information in non-formalised logbooks at the farms as well as with veterinary surgeons (particularly the lack of withdrawal periods impedes the control of legal use). - Inadequate storage of veterinary drugs on farm due to hygienically unacceptable conditions. - No professional diaries with private practising veterinary surgeons. - Private veterinary surgeon (contracted by district veterinary directorate for official tasks since 9 months) without any valid license to engage in veterinary practice. /DERUDWRU\ 6HUYLFHV *HQHUDO $VSHFWV The network of residue control laboratories is organised through one National Reference Laboratory, assisted by six regional (zonal) laboratories. Groups of residues are equally distributed all over the six zonal laboratories, even though all compounds are not screened for in all analytical laboratories. . Two laboratories have been visited during the mission: - The Institutul de Igiena si Sanatate Publica Veterinara (Institute of Hygiene and Public Health), Str. Câmpul Mosilor nr. 5, Sector 2, Bucuresti, Cod 73341, Romania (NRL for all residues); - The Zonal (Regional) Veterinary Laboratory for Residue Control, Iasi (analytical laboratory in charge of all residues for the districts of Botosani, Suceava, Neamt, Bacau, Vaslui and Iasi districts). 5.2.1.1. Staff The situation was adequate for the two visited laboratories from a quantitative point of view. In the %XFKDUHVW laboratory, the personnel are composed of 110 employees and 12 managers; one director, assisted by a deputy, manages 6 services in which 30 veterinary surgeons and more than 20 graduate chemists are employed. A post graduate chemist assumes the Quality Officer function with one person in each of the six units being her quality officer correspondent. The number of staff appeared sufficient for assuring the performance of the sample number mentioned in the plan. 6 In the ,DVL laboratory, the personnel is composed of 11 employees of which 4 are Chemist Engineers, one is a Veterinarian Doctor and 5 are chemists of different grade levels. The laboratory is divided into 4 main sections. The management of Quality Assurance of the Residue Control Activity was given to a Chemist (PhD level) in accordance with a recent Ministerial Order (5 October 2000). The number of staff appeared sufficient for assuring the performance of the sample number mentioned in the plan. From a qualitative point of view the fulfilment of continuous education related to the work to be undertaken, was generally adequate. In the Reference Laboratory in %XFKDUHVW, some of the functions were carried out by over-qualified graduates (sample reception). But, on the other hand, the insufficient number of staff strictly dedicated to methodology research and development as well as the evident absence of continuous training generates unfavourable consequences on the performance level of the method used, and finally decreases the efficiency of the national control for some veterinary drugs. In ,DVL, the continuous training of people is well assured by the NRL of Bucharest. 5.2.1.2. Building and equipment Globally, the two laboratories audited have an adequate installation, even if their age and the non air-conditioning of critical rooms do not favour analytical efficiency. The Iasi laboratory is planned to move soon. The ratio between square meters and staff numbers appears acceptable. Used analytical equipment in %XFKDUHVW is 1 GC-MS, 4 GC-ECD, 2 GC- NPD, 2 HPLC with UV and fluorescence detectors, 1 spectrophotometer, 1 atomic absorption spectrometer and ELISA reader. It corresponds at least to the minimum required for good screening efficiency. Nevertheless, mass spectrometric detection techniques would assure more sensitive and specific detection, especially for confirmatory analysis. Analytical instrumentation in ,DVL are 1 GC coupled to 2 ECD, 1 GC coupled to NPD and ECD, 1 radioactivity detector; no ELISA system is available so that some analysis must be performed outside the laboratory. This lack of Elisa-material means that the Romanian annual plan for residues is not fully performed in this lab. 5.2.1.3. Quality Assurance System An administrative decision has been taken to implement a Quality Assurance System in all Romanian residue laboratories. However, two different situations have been met: In %XFKDUHVW, a QA system was initiated several months ago. Nevertheless, the Quality Manual is still under preparation, and only few Standard Operating Procedures were available. The following observations should be taken into account: - the in-coming and out-going of people is not registered; 7 - samples are identifiable during the analytical process; - no training session planning for the staff of the laboratory is described; - no standard operating procedure nor check list for sample reception was available; - no metrological thermometer control and no register, especially for refrigerators containing official samples and standards; the technical/scientific equipment is not covered with a detailed maintenance register. The laboratory should be accredited before 2002. In ,DVL, the head of the laboratory demonstrated a voluntary approach for developing a Quality Assurance System. Nevertheless, in spite of the recent nomination of a Quality Officer, nothing has been done as yet. 5.2.1.4. Central Laboratory %XFKDUHVW Methodologies used in the laboratory are generally based on existing AOAC publications. Some of them are particularly old and generally not adapted to the situation in terms of limit of detection; as for instance in the case of unauthorised substances. Furthermore, no evidence was given to correlate the limit of detection actually reached daily and the one given in the monitoring plan programme. Traceability within the laboratory was satisfactory. Some technical deficiencies were noticed: - No formalised dossier available showing clearly either the validation of the methods or at least the demonstration of laboratory ability to reproduce results. - Since raw data are not kept even when TLC or ELISA methods are used, it is difficult to prove and to understand how the presence/absence interpretation of the target analytes was performed. - Internal standards are generally not used. In case of suspicious samples, few confirmatory methods are available. Moreover, no identification criteria are planned to be used (cf. 93/256/EC Decision), which might result in false positive results. - A procedure for characterising reference standards does not exist. The purity as well as the identity of the substance is not checked when received in the laboratory. The evaluation of the efficient fulfilment of the tasks of a NRL as described in Directive 96/23/EC showed that this laboratory almost completely executed its obligations. The laboratory organised at least one workshop a year and it assists the central administration to decide the content and organisation of the plan. Periodical comparative test for each residue group is well organised to check the performance of the regional laboratories. The 8 laboratory activity is mainly devoted to routine analysis and little time given for methodology development. Finally, it has been noted that there is only a limited participation in international organised proficiency testing schemes. 5.2.1.5. Regional Laboratories ,DVL Laboratory activities are 100% dedicated to routine residue analysis. It participates in the ring-tests organised by the Reference Laboratory. The register of the inter-laboratory evaluation is well documented. General methodologies used in the laboratory are generally the ones published by the Reference Laboratory. Nevertheless, some critical deviations have been detected. For instance, HPLC is used instead of the reference techniques GC- ECD or ELISA for steroids and a non-official protocol of extraction and purification is applied. Melengestrol acetate is not analysed despite the information given in the monitoring plan. Once again, no evidence was given to assure the limit of detection in each sample. The level in spiked control-samples should be as close as possible to the theoretical limit of detection, and not 1000 times higher as observed for -agonistic drugs. Traceability in the laboratory was satisfactory. Minor important technical deficiencies observed were: - Raw data are not kept especially when TLC is used. - Internal standards are generally not used. - There is no procedure for characterising reference standards. The purity as well as the identity of the substance is not checked when received in the laboratory. 0HDVXUHV LQ FDVH RI LQIULQJHPHQW Based on Ministerial order No 186/2000 sanctions in case of infringement can be initiated according to the severity of the case: - administrative sanctions e.g. fines or restrictions on licenses, and - criminal law sanctions like imprisonment (in collaboration with police/justice). &RQWURO IHHV All official actions ordinated by the ministry are free of charge for the animal owner and a

audits.title: Live animals & products of animal origin

recommendations.text: Fully to implement Community legislative provisions in relation to live animals and animal products intended for export to the EU.
To ensure that effective internal control systems exist, such that the performance of the official services, and controls over processing establishments, are properly monitored.
To provide additional training for Veterinary Officers and Inspectors in relation to HACCP principles, and the EU legislative requirements concerning the production of milk and milk-based products.
To ensure that goats are included in the national surveillance programme designed to demonstrate freedom from Brucella melitensis.
To operate the EBL eradication programme so that the certification provisions of Commission Decision 98/372/EC can be respected.

To develop and implement a documented system for the control of raw milk quality in respect of milk and milk products destined for EU export. This should include adequate separation from raw milk not meeting this standard.
To ensure that deficiencies found during this mission are addressed in all EU-approved establishments.

To provide the Commission services with statistics of human cases of zoonoses in 2000 (brucellosis, tuberculosis, etc.) in Romania. To submit, within three months of receiving the final report, an action plan indicating the action proposed or already taken to address the above recommendations and the conclusions of this report. This plan should include deadlines by which the proposed action will be completed. 8.2. To the Commission Services 8.2.1. To retain Romania on the existing lists of countries authorised for the export of live animals and animal products, provided that the competent authorities of Romania respond in a satisfactory manner within the set deadline to the above recommendations. ADDENDUM TO THE MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/3168/2001 The competent authorities of Romania have submitted comments on the draft report. In addition, information on the actions planned or completed in response to the recommendations, with the exception of recommendations 8.1.5. and 8.1.8., was received. 36

audits.title: Poultry meat, poultry meat products, live poultry and hatching eggs

recommendations.text: The Commission services should continue to monitor the progress of veterinary supervision in the field of poultry meat, poultry meat products production and live poultry in Romania. 36

The Commission services should not add any other establishments in Romania to the relevant list, unless the information requested under point 8.1 has been received and positively assessed. 37 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)3256/2001 Competent Authority's (CA) response to the recommendations in the report The CA of Romania has informed the FVO in their letter of 14/09/2001 that: · The correction of the deficiencies indicated has been initiated and most of them have been already rectified. · The CA has suspended from 16/03/2001 the right of exporting poultry meat products from one of the establishments visited to the EU.

audits.title: Conditions for export of live sheep and horses

recommendations.text: To take contact with the Commission services to discuss and agree the urgent corrective actions needed in relation to the identification of, and movement controls over, horses and sheep intended for export.

To carry out inspections on all authorised export stations to confirm that Community requirements in relation to animal identification and certification procedures, facilities, structures, equipment, operational practices, hygiene and animal welfare are respected, within 10 days of receiving the fax accompanying this report and immediately to submit the results of the inspection to the Commission services.
To take urgent action to address the failings in the EIA control and eradication programme.

The definition of an "epidemiological unit" needs to be more clearly defined, so that it covers all holdings in the same village, both in respect of disease controls and any subsequent slaughter actions.
National legislation on the isolation of horses or sheep in quarantine stations must be brought fully into line with EU requirements, and rigorously enforced.
To verify that compulsory sampling on export quarantine farms is not carried out only by private veterinarians. 13

To organise training for the official veterinarians and concessionary veterinarians involved in live animal exports to the EU on the animal heath requirements for these exports and on certification procedures.

To provide the Commission Services with a report on how the system of ear tagging of export sheep will be operated (provision of eartags, controls of eartags, procedures for replacement of lost eartags etc.).

To ensure that animal welfare requirements are respected on export quarantine farms and on animal transports. In particular, animals that are unfit for transport must receive veterinary treatment and be excluded from the export trade.

To inform the Commission services on progress with the implementation of horse identification with electronic microchips. To inform the Commission Services of the results of checks carried out by the official services on the operation of this system. To submit within one month of receiving this draft report an action plan with the actions proposed, or already taken, to address recommendations 8.1.3 - 8.1.10 and the conclusions of this report. This plan should include deadlines by which the proposed actions will be completed. 8.2. To the Commission Services (1) Urgently to inform the Member States of the problems encountered with the export of live sheep and equidae from Romania, so that additional border checks can be implemented. (2) To take urgent contact with the Romanian authorities to identify and agree the corrective actions required to address the serious, long-standing, problems identified in this report. (3) To confirm that the actions referred to in point (2) above have been satisfactorily implemented, and to consider whether further control measures are needed in light of this review. 9. ADDENDUM The Romanian authorities provided details of the action taken in response to recommendation 8.1.2, in a letter, received in the FVO on 14 July 2003. They indicated that all export quarantine stations had been controlled. Action had been taken, up to and including the temporary withdrawal of authorisations, in respect of 12 stations. A summary table of the outcome of these controls has been requested, and its receipt is awaited. Further checks in this sector will be undertaken during future FVO missions. The action plan for recommendations 8.1.3 ­ 8.1.10 is awaited. 14

audits.title: Conditions for export of live sheep and horses

recommendations.text: To ensure that the 30 day quarantine period for horses to be exported to the EU is rigorously enforced.
To provide training to all veterinarians involved in export certification, so that they are made fully aware of the principles of veterinary certification as laid down in Council Directive 96/93/EC4

To continue the implementation of the microchip identification system for horses and to ensure that this is completed as soon as possible. Technical data concerning the specification of microchips and readers should be provided to the Commission services and to Member States to which horses are exported.
To continue the development of identification and movement control systems for sheep in order to achieve compliance with EU requirements.
To proceed, as soon as possible, to the elimination of horses that are sero-positive for EIA.

To define, in law, an "epidemiological unit" taking into account such factors as the characteristics of farming in Romania and the degree of direct and indirect contact 4 L 013 , 16/01/1997 P. 0028 ­ 0030 Council Directive 96/93/EC of 17 December 1996 on the certification of animals and animal products 10 between animals in different ownership. This definition should then be applied within all disease control and eradication programmes. To submit within one month of receiving this draft report an action plan with the actions proposed, or already taken, to address recommendations 8.1 (1) - 8.1.(6) and the conclusions of this report. This plan should include deadlines by which proposed actions will be completed. ADDENDUM In their response to the draft report the Romanian authorities have provided initial responses to all of the recommendations made. The following is a summary of the assurances provided: Ø Legislation (MAFWE Order No. 710/24.10.2003, published in the Official Journal of Romania Part I, No. 688/1.10.2003), requiring a 30 day pre-export quarantine period for equines, came into force on 15 October 2003 and is being enforced. Ø Training will be provided to veterinarians, who provide export certification for live animals, in February and May 2004. Ø 80% of equines infected with Equine Infectious Anaemia have been identified by means of microchips. Information on the specification of these microchips was provided. Ø Identification and registration of sheep, goats and pigs will be carried out in 2004. A schedule of activities, including tendering for software & tags and distribution and application of tags was provided. Ø The elimination of EIA sero-positive equines will start in February 2004. Owners will receive compensation for compulsorily slaughtered horses. Ø Clarification on the interpretation and application of the term "epidemiological unit" was provided. 11

audits.title: Identification/certification live Sheep and Horses

recommendations.text: To ensure that the 30 day quarantine period for horses to be exported to the EU is rigorously enforced
To ensure that certifying officials act fully in accordance with the principles of veterinary certification
To implement an effective control system to detect and correct failures in the certification procedures and in the approval of quarantine stations.
To implement, as soon as possible, the official identification of sheep, goats and horses.
To proceed to eliminate horses sero-positive to EIA.
To ensure that the correct certificate model for sheep is appropriately completed.

To inspect all quarantine facilities and procedures to ensure that they meet all conditions for certification of live animals for export to the EU. To submit within one month of receiving this draft report an action plan with the actions planned, or already taken, to address these recommendations. This plan should include deadlines by which the planned actions will be completed. 9. ADDENDUM On 23 August 2004 the Romanian CCA provided the FVO with the immediate actions taken and an action plan to address the recommendations made. The operating licence of the farm visited during the mission in Covasna County has been withdrawn and disciplinary measures were taken against the official veterinarians responsible for its control. Training for veterinarians with responsibilities in the export of live animals took place between 5 July and 10 August 2004. Only veterinarians achieving high marks in the final test are permitted to certify exports of live animals. The CCA sent instructions to the counties about the models of certificate to be used and their completion, according to Commission Decision 2004/212/EC. The CCA stated that the correct models are in use since 7 July 2004. 12

audits.title: Residues and contaminants, including controls on veterinary medicinal products

recommendations.text: Ensure that the NRCP covers all relevant substances insofar as they relate to exported commodities. As a matter of urgency particular attention should be paid to ensuring that analyses are carried out in order to guarantee exported commodities do not contain detectable residues of those substances presently listed in Annex IV to Council Regulation (EEC) No 2377/90 or not listed in annexes I, II, or III of said Regulation. Laboratories

Ensure that in respect of guarantees on the residue status of animals and animal products exported to the EU, laboratory analytical methods should be: properly validated (fit for purpose); preferably carried out within the scope of accreditation to ISO 17025; and capable of demonstrating compliance with Community limits. VMPs and medicated feedingstuffs

To immediately rectify the observed deficiencies in relation to the availability and marketing of VMPs and improve existing controls on all stages of the VMP distribution chain in order to: a. comply with national (i.e. transposed Community) legislation; b. detect illegal or unauthorised treatment of animals liable to be exported to the EU and; c. ensure that residues of substances not authorised in the EU are not present in animals and animal products exported to the EU.

Implement without delay the (already transposed) equine passport system in respect of all equidae liable to be exported to the EU in order to ensure the traceability and provide the necessary information on residue status of such animals. 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 7762/2005 In their letter of 5 August 2005 in response to the draft report, the Romanian CA did not comment on the content of the report, nevertheless they provided already an action plan on the recommendations made in the draft report. The response can be summarised as follows: With regard to NRCP: Recommendation 1: It is planned to increase the scope of analysis for several substance groups in 2006 (e.g. for A3, A5, A6 (nitroimidazoles), B1, B2a, B2b, B2c, B2e and B3e). With regard to laboratories: Recommendation 2: A time table has been provided in order to have all laboratories accredited at the latest in 2006. This table also includes an indication of the completion of the validation studies, according to Commission Decision 2002/657/EC, and the accreditation for a number of methods. Furthermore, reinforcement of additional qualified laboratory staff and analytical equipment is intended in IHVPH. 9 With regard to VMPs and medicated feedingstuffs: Recommendation 3: a. An action plan has started in order to review the labels and the usage conditions of the VMPs. The implementation of this review will be finalised by 1 October 2005. b. Elaboration of legal acts will take place before 1 September 2005. The implementation of these measures will be done until 1 June 2006. Supervision of the implementation measures is also foreseen, together with a reporting per trimester. c. The control is carried out by the veterinarians taking care of pharmacovigilance, within county DSVA and will be reported each trimester, in accordance with the inspection calendar. Recommendation 4: Action is in course of development. Deadline: 1 January 2006. _________________

audits.title: Avian Influenza

recommendations.text: The CCA should consistently report all AI outbreaks detected to the Commission Services (Art.3 of Decision 93/342/EC).

The CCA should consider adapting the stamping out policy in light of the experience acquired since the start of the epidemic. 6.4. Surveillance and epidemiological studies The CCA should endeavour to improve the surveillance plan by better clarifying the poultry population to be monitored and testing methods to be used 15 The mission team was informed at the final meeting that the diagnostic protocols had been reviewed and a copy of the new protocols was handed over to the team for consideration. 15 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/8305/2006 In their reply to the draft report dated 19 April 2006, the Romanian CA responded to some of the recommendations and findings. In particular concerning the following recommendations: 6.1 Structure and organisation of CA CAs stated that they are currently seeking to purchase a building to accommodate 300 people. 6.2 Laboratories CAs stated that a chart of diagnostic methods, a copy of which had been handed to the mission team (see footnote no.15), has been sent to the EU Community Reference Laboratory for assessment. They also stated that the result of this assessment will be sent to the Commission Services. An ELISA test has been introduced in the diagnostic protocol for Anatides to be used as a screening method in the local laboratories. 6.3.2 Measures in case of confirmation The stamping out policy has been defined in the legal Order no. 87/2006. Concerning some of the findings CAs stated that the operational manual and protocols to complete the contingency plan will be published in September 2006 and that the epidemiological forms for enquires in epidemic areas has been established by the legal Order no.87/2006.

audits.title: GMO - Controls on food and feed

recommendations.text: Proceed urgently with plans to fully transpose Directive 2001/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council. 17

Until such time as the threshold values for GMO in seed are set under Article 21 of Directive 2001/18/EC, ensure that national legislation on the adventitious presence of GMO in seed lots is brought into line with the practice of using the analytical limit of detection.
Ensure that food and feed produced from GM soya fulfils the requirements of Articles 12 and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003.

Extend official control activities to include products potentially containing additional authorised GMO and non authorised GMO to comply with the requirements of Articles 4.2 and 16.2 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003.

Ensure that the central ISDA laboratory is sufficiently resourced in order to comply with the requirements for National Reference Laboratories as specified by Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Ensure that the ISDA laboratory can adequately analyse additional authorised GMO (under Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003) in order to comply with the requirements of Article 9.1 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003. 10. COMPETENT AUTHORITY RESPONSE TO RECOMMENDATIONS

audits.title: Controls on Feed and compliance with requirements for Feed Hygiene

recommendations.text: To communicate and coordinate, as required by Art. 4 (5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, as far as necessary with other CAs responsible for primary producers of feed.

To document the process of drafting the official control programme, in order to demonstrate that official controls are carried out on a risk basis, as laid down in Art. 3 (1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To ensure that comparative tests organised in line with Art. 33 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, ensure that those laboratories carrying out official analyses for feed are able to undertake their duties satisfactorily. 14 DG(SANCO)/2007-7273 ­ MR Final
To make progress in the process of registration laid down by Art. 9 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, notably concerning primary producers of feed.
To take actions to ensure that, as of January 2008, all FBOs comply with the conditions laid down in Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, as required in its Art. 18.

To carry out effective official controls to ensure compliance with the requirements for HACCP systems laid down in Art. 6 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and for quality controls, laid down in Annex II to the said Regulation.

To carry out physical checks on imported feedingstuffs at a frequency depending on the risks associated with different feed and the history of compliance of the country or establishment of origin, as required by Art. 16 (2) of Regulation EC) No 882/2004.

The authorise imports only under the conditions laid down in Art. 6 of Directive 98/51/EC, establishing a list of representatives in the EU of establishments located in third countries, and their declaration of compliance with EU requirements for feed hygiene.

To reinforce official controls (concerning both the substances analyses and the premises from which samples are taken) to ensure compliance with the phasing out of antibiotics as feed additives laid down by Art. 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2004.

To reinforce compliance with the rules on undesirable substances laid down Directive 2002/32/EC (notably for those that are not currently tested) in order to ensure that the maximum levels set out in Annex II are not exceeded. _______________________________________ COMPETENT AUTHORITY RESPONSE TO RECOMMENDATIONS

audits.title: Import/Transit Controls and Border Inspection Posts

recommendations.text: To complete transposition of EU import legislation which applied pre- accession, in particular the translation of model health certificates into Romanian language and to repeal any existing National legislation not coherent with directly applicable Regulations and Decisions.

In view of the fact that non-EU-complying POAO may be introduced on the Romanian territory since accession and to avoid problems should this eventuality arise, to allocate competencies for approval or authorization and supervision of customs warehouses and ship suppliers in order to be in a position to apply the requirements of Artt. 12 and 13 of Directive 97/78/EC.

To develop adequate administrative arrangements for veterinary checks and supervision of non-EU complying consignments in transit, in free zones, customs warehouses or ship suppliers, so as to correctly apply Artt. 11, 12 and 13 of Directive 97/78/EC. Additionally to put in place suitable administrative arrangements to correctly apply the provisions of Decision 2007/29/EC

To review all instructions and manuals in order to determine what supplementary guidance is required in order to provide sufficiently clear guidance to allow correct implementation of veterinary checks ­ including animal welfare requirements and quarantine of commercial birds other than poultry ­ and so as to adequately implement Art. 8.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and section 3 of the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC.

To take measures to ensure that documentation, in particular model health certificates, is maintained at the BIPs as required in section 3 of the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC and to ensure that all staff are aware of which documentation they require in order to be able to properly implement the import requirements for live animals and animal products in order to correctly execute the checks foreseen in Directives 91/496/EEC and 97/78/EC.

recommendations.text: To ensure that only establishments complying with the requirements of Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 are approved, that conditional approval is granted in a harmonised way and that all activities of integrated establishments are listed.

To review the situation regarding availability of laboratory capacity, equipment and quality of performance in order to ensure the performance of official sampling according to the national strategic plan and sampling of raw materials and potable water as part of own control programmes to comply with Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and Council Directive 98/83/EC respectively.

To ensure that fresh meat produced in approved slaughterhouses complies with hygiene rules, is inspected as laid down in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and meets eligibility criteria specified in Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073 and 2075/2005.

audits.title: Pesticides

recommendations.text: The CAs should implement audit systems as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CAs should ensure that there is efficient and effective coordination between 2 all competent authorities carrying out official controls in accordance with Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The MPH should provide appropriate training for the inspectors concerning 3 controls of pesticide residues in food of plant origin as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 4 The MPH should ensure that the ASPs of all counties have access to appropriate laboratory capacity for analysis of pesticide residues in baby food. The CAs should ensure that the NRLs work closely together, so as to ensure 5 efficient coordination between them, with other national laboratories and the CRLs in accordance with 33(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CAs should ensure that all laboratories responsible for pesticide residue analysis in food of plant origin have appropriate and properly maintained 6 equipment to ensure that staff can perform official controls effectively and efficiently as required by Article 4 (1)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The quality control system in the laboratories availing of Article 18 should be based on the Method validation and quality control procedures for pesticide residue analysis in food and feed Document No SANCO 2007/3131. audits.title: Salmonella National Control Programme in particular poultry populations

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that only adequately trained staff perform official controls on the implementation of the SNCP as required under Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The CA should ensure that laboratories involved in the SNCP participate regularly in proficiency testing in line with Article 12 point 2 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003 to ensure reliable test results.

The CA should ensure that laboratories involved in the SNCP apply quality assurance systems that conform to EN ISO/IEC 17025 standards as required by Article 12 point 1b of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003, in particularly ensuring adequate samples traceability and timely reporting of positive results.
The CCA should gather the necessary up-to-date information in order to carry out an adequate review and evaluation of the SNCP in line with Article 5.3.d of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003.

The CA should ensure that the activities carried out under the Salmonella monitoring programme and the results thereof, are made available to the public as required under Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
The CA should guarantee that in cases of non-compliance action will be taken to ensure that the operator remedies the situation as required under Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004).
The CA should ensure that all poultry farms comply with the requirements of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

The CA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in breeding flocks complies with the requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 2160/2003 and 200/2010, in particular as regards number of samples taken, sampling frequency and action taken after a positive test result.

The CA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in laying flocks complies with the requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 2160/2003 and1168/2006, in particular as regards number of samples taken, action following positive test result and the policy to be followed in the case of positive dust but negative faecal samples.

The CA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in broiler flocks complies with the requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 2160/2003 and 646/2007, in particular as regards sampling rules to cover all flocks of broilers.
The CA should ensure that the food chain information includes the results of samples taken in the framework of the SNCP as required by Annex II, Section III, point 3e of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

recommendations.text: The CA should draw up operational contingency plans setting out measures to be implemented without delay when food (fishery products) is found to present a serious risk to humans. The contingency plans should be in place, and the CA should be prepared to operate such plans in the event of an emergency (see Article 4 (f) and Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004).

The CA should guarantee that the procedure used when enforcement measures shall be applied ensures that action is taken to force the operator to remedy the situation (see Article 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004).

Findings

The audit team noted that the competent authority relies on Customs to identify transhipped consignments where the BIP of entry is in Romania and direct them to the BIP. The audit team found two consignments destined for Romania which had been issued with transhipment CVEDs by BIPs in other Member States. Both consignments were incorrectly released for free circulation by Customs when they arrived in Romania as Customs did not know the difference between different types of CVEDs and BIPs in Romania were not involved in either case. The competent authority stated that the procedure for transhipments is currently in draft stage. The audit team noted that the relevant EU Commission guideline was not available at this BIP. 4

There is a lack of available procedures in some cases (e.g. procedures for screening of manifests and/or Customs database, transhipments) and the competent authority has not taken into account all the relevant monitoring parameters in the preparation of the 5 monitoring plan. citations.text: In two of the BIPs visited (port, airport), staff stated that they carry out cross-checks between data available on the Customs database and transport manifests in order to verify that no imports violate the requirements of Article 4 (1) of Directive 91/496/EEC and Article 3 of Directive 97/78/EC. This process includes screening 100% of manifests to identify consignments which may contain products of animal origin. The audit team randomly selected seven examples from the files to assess the system, as follows: A consignment of live birds originating from a third country and coming from another Member State was highlighted in the manifest hard copy by BIP staff. However, there was no evidence on file of any follow-up/cross check with the Customs database in order to identify whether this consignment was subject to veterinary check or had already been checked in the previous Member State. The competent authority contacted Customs at the time of the FVO audit and established that the consignment had a CVEDA. Two consolidated consignments selected by the audit team for which ''product of animal origin'' was highlighted on the manifests by BIP staff but there was no follow-up to identify whether there were consignments subject to veterinary check. BIP staff stated that they check 100% of manifests and identify consignments of products of animal origin on the manifests. However, they do not follow these up or ensure that they are 3 subject to BIP checks. The BIPs rely on Customs identifying all consignments on the positive list which require veterinary checks. The CN codes of products listed in Commission Decision 2007/275/EC are flagged in the Customs database and Customs require a CVED in order to lift the flag and release such consignments.

Two of the BIPs (port, airport) visited had access to the Customs database. However staff were only using this access to follow-up veterinary consignments when there was a specific question (e.g. to check if the consignments in transit had left the country). There was no cross-check to verify whether all consignments that required veterinary inspection had been presented to the BIP.

The road BIP visited had no access to the Customs database. The competent authority stated that this was due to a lack of compatibility of the local IT system with the Customs database. According to the competent authority the issue had remained outstanding for approximately five months and at the time of the FVO audit no action had been planned to address it. The audit team noted that there are approximately 1,000 consignments that pass through this border point each month and the lack of screening of the available information to identify consignments subject to veterinary inspection, may lead to a situation in which such consignments enter the EU without undergoing veterinary checks.

In the three BIPs visited there was no written procedure on how to use the available information (screening of manifests, monitoring of Customs database) to identify consignments that should be subject to veterinary inspection. 5.2.2 Veterinary checks Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Council Directive 91/496/EEC, Council Directive 97/78/EC, Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Commission Decision 94/360/EC, Commission Decision 97/794/EC, Commission Decision 2000/208/EC, Commission Decision 2000/25/EC and Commission Decision 2001/812/EC. Findings

The system for import controls covers the consignments presented at the BIPs and the official controls are generally performed correctly. However, the competent authority does not use available information (Customs database, manifests) to ensure that all consignments subject to veterinary control are presented to the BIPs and there is partial enforcement of the requirement to notify the goods prior to arrival at the BIPs.

There is a lack of available procedures in some cases (e.g. procedures for screening of manifests and/or Customs database, transhipments) and the competent authority has not taken into account all the relevant monitoring parameters in the preparation of the 5 monitoring plan. These reduce the effectiveness of the official import controls in preventing non-compliant consignments from entering the EU. 5.3 VERIFICATION ACTIVITIES Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

audits.title: evaluate the use of the TRACES system

recommendations.text: ure that staff at LVUs enter data into TRACES as required by Article 3(2) of Directive 2004/292/EC, including the results of official controls on consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination (e.g. intra-EU movements of animals for slaughter, certain animal by-products, channelled consignments, animals passing through Control Posts).Recommendation based on conclusion 42. Associated findings: 24, 25, 29 and 35-37.

citations.text: Figures from the TRACES database indicate that 24 consignments were channelled from EU BIPs to destinations in Romania during the 18 months prior to this audit. Receipt at destination was confirmed by completing box 41 of the CVED in 12 of these cases.
There were five re-imported consignments during the same period and three had been confirmed as received at destination via completed box 41. 5 5.2.7.2 At the point of introduction

There are three Control Posts approved in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 1255/97 in Romania. There are no instructions for recording official controls carried out at Control Posts in TRACES and officials do not record such controls in TRACES. 5.2.9 INTRA module

There is no national instruction that official controls related to ante-mortem inspection for animals arriving from other Member States should be recorded in TRACES (18% of such consignments had those controls recorded during 2013 in TRACES but according to the competent authority all consignments would have been subject to ante-mortem controls).

A national instruction on the implementation of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 requires that TRACES should be used to confirm receipt at destination of category 3 animal by-products arriving from other Member States. However, it does not include a similar requirement for Categories 1 and 2 animal by-products which are also included in Article 48(3) of Regulation EC (No) 1069/2009. According to the TRACES database, less than 20% of arriving consignments of processed animal protein and categories 1 and 2 in the DOCOM module were recorded in TRACES as being controlled at destination during 2013. It was not possible to confirm what percentage of consignments were actually controlled at destination.
Many consignments rejected by BIPs and sent for destruction were not recorded in box 41 of the CVED in TRACES as being received at destination and there is no instruction on this. 5.2.10 DOCOM module

Most CVEDs, INTRA-certificates and DOCOMs are issued correctly in Romania. However, for many consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination, TRACES is not used in compliance with the legal requirements for ensuring traceability, e.g. consignments arriving from other Member States (slaughter animals, animal by- products) and imports (reimports and channelled consignments). The impact of the shortcomings is limited as some controls are implemented but not recorded in TRACES. The system of randomly checking notifications related to arriving products does not ensure that the LVU is aware of all consignments which require follow-up. Feedback received from other Member States in TRACES is not always followed up in accordance with planned arrangements and therefore increases the chances of recurrence of the original issue. 7 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal Requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that controls, at all levels but particularly at county level, are carried out in accordance with procedures in place and to ensure that corrective actions are taken when necessary as required by Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To ensure that only establishments in compliance with all the relevant requirements of food law are approved and listed as required by Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To enhance the effectiveness of official controls so as to ensure that food businesses comply with the general and specific hygiene requirements of Regulations (EC) No 852/2004 and (EC) No 853/2004 and that timely and effective corrective action is taken and documented in cases where deficiencies have been identified.

To improve the verification of Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points-based systems in order to ensure that they are implemented and in line with the requirements in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.
To ensure that post-mortem inspection is carried out in accordance with the specific requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Annex I, Section IV.
To ensure that health marks are not applied to carcasses with deficiencies that could make the meat unfit for human consumption in accordance with Article 5 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

To ensure that the protection of animals at the time of slaughter or killing is in compliance with Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 and that during stunning operations appropriate back-up equipment is immediately available on the spot and is used in the case of failure of the stunning equipment initially used as required in Article 9 of the Regulation.

To review the requirements imposed on small establishments and to apply the range of permissible flexibilities where appropriate, in particular those permitted by Annex I, Chapter 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 related to microbiological sampling of carcasses.

citations.text: The CA has tools in place to facilitate the monitoring of the implementation of the official and own-check sampling (database, auditing and reporting system) and review and evaluate the progress of the SNCPs. However there are weaknesses in the system as it does not allow the central level to monitor CSVFSDs and CSVFSLs performance and consequently to guarantee that the activities contained in the SNCPs are implemented as described in the programmes themselves. In fact, shortcomings related to sampling frequency and sampling procedures in own-checks detected by the audit team had not been identified/recorded by the official staff at county level and therefore they were not communicated from the county level to the central one. In addition, inconsistency at county level as regards the follow-up actions taken following Salmonella positive results 12 (i.e. antimicrobial sampling in case of confirmatory sampling in laying hen population and imposition of restrictive measures) had not been identified by the CA at central level. 5.4 SNCP FOR BREEDERS Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 200/2010. Audit findings

Procedures are in place for the rejection of non-compliant samples collected under the programmes. However, at county level, there are shortcomings in their implementation and this has entailed as a consequence that non-compliant samples have been accepted by the laboratories for analysis. This is not in line with EU requirements and with the approved SNCPs. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION SNCPs are implemented in Romania and cover all relevant poultry populations. An effort has been made by the CA to improve the situation since the last FVO audit in 2010. The implementation of the programmes is supported by a dedicated database and a reporting system which enables the competent authority to evaluate and review their progress. Some of the shortcomings detected during internal audits carried out in all counties on SNCPs in 2012 are similar to some of those identified by the FVO audit team but which had not been followed up and rectified. The activities and measures contained in the SNCPs are not always implemented as described in the programmes concerned. Due to weaknesses of the system in place which do not allow the CA at central level to monitor the performance of official staff at county level, 21 shortcomings still exist concerning sampling frequency and procedures of own-checks that are not identified at county level and therefore not reported to the central level. In addition, some of the required follow-up actions after Salmonella positive results are not taken by relevant officials. Other issues concern biosecurity controls, confirmatory sampling practices and eggs that may be sent directly for human consumption despite flocks having proved positive for Salmonella based on an official dust sample test. 7. CLOSING MEETING During the closing meeting held in Bucharest on 12 June 2015, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit to the CA. The CA acknowledged the FVO's findings. 8. recommendations.text: Ensure that the comprehensive documented procedures are in place for official controls on the storage of vaccine to verify that cold-chain requirements are strictly adhered to and to take corrective actions when needed. Article 8(1) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion No 20. Associated finding No 15.

citations.text: Official controls of vaccine storage were carried out in accordance with the CCA instructions but these instructions were incomplete: The CCA informed the audit team that the representatives of the technical commission were permanently present at the airfield during vaccine distribution2. Temperature records regarding the bait storage conditions during 2014 campaign were checked by the technical commission (official veterinarian) once per day during vaccine distribution and the records of the official checks were available. The audit team reviewed the instance when temperature records from the thermometers in the freezing container showed deviation from the established limit (a rise of temperature from -20o C up to -1.2 o C due to a power cut). The deviation was noted by the contractor only after more than 24 hours and the CA was notified. During this 24 hours period, aerial distribution was not carried out. The batches stored inside this container were sampled and re-tested for virus titre in the Institute for Control of Veterinary Biological Products and Medicines. The test results were compliant with contract criteria. The procedure in place did not define the frequency of official temperature controls, and the critical point (combination of raised temperature above limit with maximum allowed time) was not included either.

The adequate pre-distribution quality checks on vaccine batches ensure the quality of the vaccine when it is distributed. The incomplete procedures in place to demonstrate maintenance of the cold chain for baits point to certain weaknesses in the control practices.

citations.text: Sampling of foxes to monitor vaccine uptake and fox population immunity was seriously under-implemented and unevenly geographically distributed in 2013-2014: The following table summarises laboratory data for foxes sampled in calendar years 2013 and 2014 Year Rabies cases Number of foxes tested for % tested foxes % tested foxes in contact vaccinated Rabies virus Tetracycline Antibodies with bait 10 2013 286* 2755* 1638 1387 15.32% (251) 9.95% (138) 2014 95* 2269* 2165 2022 27.67% (599) 28.04% (567) For rabies* total numbers under active and passive surveillance In 2013 and 2014 none of the 41 counties met their target of number of planned samples - four foxes /100 Km2 per year (representing approx. 8,500 foxes shot in Romania). Only 0.86 foxes / 100 Km2 were tested for tetracycline and 0.73 foxes /100 Km2 were tested for antibodies in 2013. In 2014 those figures slightly increased to 1.01 foxes / 100 Km2 and 0.95 foxes /100 Km2 respectively, but still were well below the targets. In 2014 the sampling for tetracycline varied between the counties, ranging from 0.1 up to 2.4 foxes /100 Km2. In one county visited, out of 170 foxes tested for rabies virus, only 64 were tested for tetracycline and rabies antibodies under the monitoring scheme. By permitting to use only foxes shot within a 60 days sampling window, all other foxes shot during the year become ineligible for monitoring. The majority of foxes were shot to regulate fox population density and the carcases were sent directly to the rendering plant without laboratory examination.

The monitoring of vaccine uptake and population immunity in 2013-2014 was inadequate. The 60 days sampling window applied after vaccination campaign limits the possibility to increase the number of samples. However there has been a significant improvement in sampling after the autumn campaign 2014 as a result of new CA legal powers to enforce sampling by the hunters and more active involvement of the CA.
The supervision from central level during the monitoring period does not ensure that sampling targets will be met in all counties.

Data collected shall be complete, verified and detailed enough to allow comprehensive analysis. Points 6(c) and 7(a)(b) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC. citations.text: The procedures of age determination of the monitored foxes were not detailed enough and the determination was based on an insufficiently accurate method: 3 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that for 2014 campaign they reached the target for sampling with a total of 3,826 foxes shot and tested for tetracycline and for antibodies by ELISA test. The target for sampling was 6965 foxes for both campaigns envisaged in 2014. In 2015 they intend to shoot planned number of foxes - 8535 (4 foxes/100 square kilometres) and complete their testing for evaluation of the effectiveness of vaccination in 2015. The same annual targets are planned for the whole period 2015-2017 (Romanian eligible area for the oral vaccination of foxes is 213,375 km2, so the total yearly number for shooting in 2 campaigns is 8375 foxes). 11 No clear cut-off between the category of young foxes (cubs) and adults is set up by the CCA and thereby the age threshold in the counties visited varied between 12 and 15 months. The age determination only by visual inspection of carcases, in particular after autumn campaign, is not providing sufficiently reliable results. The young foxes are already 8-9 months old and grown up which makes visual age classification very difficult. The age has not been verified by more specific laboratory method. 5.3.2 Active/targeted surveillance

Passive surveillance varies between the counties and is inadequate in several counties. The data available are not comprehensive enough to fully assess the effectiveness of passive surveillance: Although requested by the audit team, the CCA did not provided data on the number of foxes tested and found positive for rabies virus broken down by type of surveillance (active; passive). The numbers of suspect cases (tested under passive surveillance) were provided by the CCA per county and per calendar year, but no further details (e.g. numbers broken down by different category of indicator animals such as animals killed with clinical signs, found dead or road-kills), were available. In 2014, 252 suspect samples were tested for rabies (mainly dogs, foxes, cats, bovines, and other species). The number of suspect cases varied between the counties. In six counties and Bucharest municipality no suspect case was reported. recommendations.text: To ensure that BIPs have appropriate equipment to guarantee that staff can perform official controls efficiently and effectively as required in Article 4(2) Recommendation based on conclusions 22 and 50. Associated findings: 11, 15 and 48.

citations.text: BIPs have appropriate and properly maintained facilities in compliance with the requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC. However, BIPs do not have proper equipment to perform physical checks, including sampling, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (see section 5.5). Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan

Even though the monitoring plan requires the taking of samples for microbiological examination, the BIPs visited did not have proper equipment (see section 5.5) to implement the physical checks and the sterility. In accordance with the written procedures, BIPs take the extra sample for the supplementary opinion (if required by the operator), however those samples were stored sealed in BIP facilities without proper labelling. Therefore, sampling and handling of samples in BIPs did not follow the requirements of Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. BIPs store both samples until the person responsible for the load collects them for transportation to the laboratory concerned.

The implementation of the monitoring plan is undermined due to deficiencies in targeting consignments, the lack of equipment for sampling and transportation of samples to the laboratories. Therefore, the implementation of the monitoring plan does not fully achieve the objective of the monitoring plan.

The audit team noted that inspection rooms were not equipped with the necessary technical equipment for performing identity and physical checks contrary to the requirements of Article 2(1) and Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC: A thermometer to measure surface temperature and sterile bags were not available and a core thermometer was out of order at inspection centre "IC1" of Albia BIP. 11 A core thermometer, a saw, and sterile bags were not available at Constana South ­ Agigea BIP. However the lack of communication between those involved in the development and implementation of the monitoring plan, combined with the lack of a mechanism to ensure flexibility in its implementation, reduces the effectiveness of the monitoring plan in overseeing that imported goods comply with EU requirements. Deficiencies in the selection of consignments to be tested, lack of equipment for sampling and the fact that samples are transported to the laboratories by the persons responsible for the load collectively weaken the implementation of the monitoring plan and fulfilment of its objective. Whilst verification is in place to check the progress of implementation of import controls (including sampling), the verification activities do not cover the appropriateness of the samples taken nor do they lead to the actions to improve the implementation of the monitoring plan. Therefore, the verification of the implementation was not able to identify deficiencies which undermine the overall effectiveness of the monitoring plan. Sampling in case of suspicion is limited to following safeguard measures and imposed checks. The absence of further sampling under suspicion, together with the limited implementation of the monitoring plan, undermines the ability of the competent authority to detect consignments for which the veterinary legislation might have been not complied with or for which there is doubt. The use of RASFF by the Import Directorate and BIPs is limited, therefore it cannot be used for consultation to identify the possible suspicious consignments. The re-enforced checks regime is implemented in compliance with the applicable requirements. RASFF notifications are correctly followed by BIPs when triggered by other Member States due to the information received using TRACES. Even though the facilities at all locations visited by the audit team comply with EU requirements, equipment is not fully fit for purpose for the categories included in their approval and may compromise the hygienic sampling and handling of the consignments subject to veterinary checks. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 11 December 2015 with the representatives from NSVFSA and Customs. recommendations.text: To ensure that the minimum number of isolates derived from turkey caecal samples required by point 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU is subject to antimicrobial susceptibility testi based on conclusion No 28 Associated finding No 20

citations.text: In 2014 and 2016 the number of caecal samples to be taken from turkey slaughterhouses was not calculated correctly. This is because for this calculation, the only turkey slaughterhouse in the country was treated as a broiler slaughterhouse. As a result, the number of samples allocated for turkey ceca was significantly lower than the one necessary to obtain the required isolates. This does not meet the requirements of point 2.2 of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

The competent authority has documented procedures in place to support the implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, delays in the inception of the sampling plan, shortcomings in the proportional allocation of samples and in the selection of the epidemiological units to be sampled, undermine the representativeness of the samples taken. 5.2.2 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

responses.response: For 2017 the Decision Grant for Antimicrobial Resistance cision monitoring provides sampling slaughterhouse and retail samples from pigs and bovines. For the year of 2018, when sampling will address poultry and turkeys, the National Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Authority will implement, in relation to point 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, a separate allocation of samples for turkeys than for broilers, so that the minimum number of isolates for turkeys will be obtained.

recommendations.text: To ensure that sampling at slaughterhouses is representative, as required by Article 2(1) and point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, in particular by randomly selecting sampling dates and avoiding repeatedly sampling the same epidemiological units. Recommendation based on conclusion No 28 Associated findings No 21, 22, 23, and 26 13

citations.text: Contrary to the requirements set out in part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, the AMR monitoring programme did not ensure that samples were distributed over each month of the year. Instead, monthly sampling took place from March to December in 2014 and from May to December in 2015 and 2016. The competent authority informed the audit team that the monitoring plan was issued only when the Grant Decision, which details the EU funds that would become available for co-financing of the plan, was published. NSVFSA stated that they will consider the possibility to have bi-annual financial plans to avoid this issue reoccurring.

The annual Service Notices state that sampling days should be limited from Monday to Wednesday to ensure that the laboratory starts processing the samples within 48 hours of collection. In the slaughterhouses visited, officials took most of the samples on Mondays. This cannot be considered random and therefore is not in line with point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU.

The Service Notices state that repeated epidemiological units cannot be sampled. Nevertheless, the epidemiological unit definition given therein is not fully in line with Decision 2013/652/EU. As a consequence, in two of the three slaughterhouses visited, the audit team noticed a few examples of repeated epidemiological units sampled. This is not in line with point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

According to the explanation provided by NSVFSA on this issue, the decision to select these counties was mainly based on the consumption of fresh meat therein. However, 6 the competent authorities did not present any consumption data to show that the actual county selection ensured representativeness. Moreover, the audit team noted that the population in the selected counties was far below the 80% required by EFSA guidance document 2014 representing 54% and 49% for 2015 and 2016, respectively. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that as required by Article 2.2 and point 1 of part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, the isolates obtained were representative.

The competent authority has documented procedures in place to support the implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, delays in the inception of the sampling plan, shortcomings in the proportional allocation of samples and in the selection of the epidemiological units to be sampled, undermine the representativeness of the samples taken. 5.2.2 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that sprouting establishments are approved as required by Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013. Recommendation based on conclusion 16 Associated findings: 12 and 13

citations.text: The NSVFSA informed the audit team that currently legal obstacles in Romanian legislation make it impossible to approve sprouting establishments as required by Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013. The NSVFSA expects that this impediment to approval will be removed by July 2016.

Sprouting establishments are registered based on a procedure established in Chapter III "Production of food of non-animal origin" of NSVFSA Order no. 111/2008, and included in Chapter III - Annex 9 ­ "Production of food of non-animal origin". The Food Business Operator (FBO) must submit an application to the CSVFSD. The application contains: a written request, the plan of the establishment, a copy of the registration certificate issued by the Commerce Register or other documents specific for the organisation form, and a copy of the identity card of the owner or legal representative of the establishment. The CSVFSD inspectors perform a documentary check and an on-site visit in order to verify the compliance with legislation on food safety. The inspectors complete a report in which they can propose not to register the FBO, in case of non-compliance with food safety legislation. If this is the case, the inspection report will set remedial measures and terms for compliance.

Legislation concerning registration is in place for sprout producers setting out the legal requirements for approval, however, this is not in compliance with Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013. 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
