audits.title: Animal health - identification and traceability of equidae

recommendations.text: The Competent Authorities should ensure that replacement identification documents are issued for equidae not identified within the time limits and that Part II of Section II of these documents is marked as not intended for slaughter for human consumption as required by Article 32(2)(c) of Regulation 2015/262. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 45. Associated findings Nos. 17, 19, 26, 27 & 28.

citations.text: ANZ confirmed it is not currently possible to print a replacement identification document from database. Consequently, equidae not identified by 12 months of age are issued a standard identification document with no associated restrictions.

Equidae which are issued a duplicate or replacement identification document are not excluded from the food chain contrary to the requirements of Articles 29(2)(c) and 32(2)(c) of Regulation 2015/262. Identification verification (Transponder)

The audit team reviewed two veterinary health certificates (from the previous week) for movement of horses from traders to the slaughterhouse visited, covering 20 and 11 animals respectively. 15 animals in the first, and six in the second, had consecutive transponder numbers. Seven consecutive numbers were checked on ANZ database and all of them had corresponding identification documents issued 1-2 days before slaughter of which two were issued to horses greater than 2 years old. CA agreed that horses with consecutive numbers had been identified at traders holding and had moved there from holding of birth with no identification.

The audit team reviewed 10 passports returned from equidae slaughtered in March 2016 from the slaughterhouse visited. Three were duplicate passports and two were "original" passports (issued for the first time). The ages of the animals ranged from 1 to 15 years old. In eight of the ten, the outline diagram had not been completed and no photograph or print depicting the animals was available.

The audit team checked data held on ANZ database relating to five horses from a holding approved under Commission Decision 2010/346/EU (and visited by audit team). In the week prior to visit, one horse had been identified and issued with a passport for 6 the first time at 5 years of age. A second horse was re-identified and issued a duplicate passport.

Weaknesses exist in the system to issue equine identification documents. These do not contain all the required information and are frequently issued with no regard to the lifetime treatment of horses with veterinary medicinal products or the animals' age. Together with incomplete FCI, this results in ineligible animals entering the food chain. Additionally, late identification results in an unknown number of horses not being tested for EIA in accordance with national surveillance programme requirements.

recommendations.text: The Competent Authorities should ensure that when duplicate identification documents are issued for equidae, Part II of Section II of these documents is marked as not intended for slaughter for human consumption or Part III of Section II is marked to suspend their eligibility for human consumption for 6 months as required by Articles 29 and 31 of Regulation 2015/262 respectively. Recommendation based on conclusion No.45. Associated findings Nos.18, 19 & 29.

citations.text: ANZ stated they did not have the technical knowledge to complete the administration of veterinary medicinal products section when issuing duplicate / replacement identification documents. They considered this a responsibility of NSVFSA but no mechanism exists to notify NSVFSA when duplicate / replacement identification documents are issued. Consequently, duplicate equine identification documents issued by ANZ do not have the section on administration of veterinary medicinal products completed. This lack of coordination between NSVFSA and ANZ is not in compliance with Article 4(3) of Regulation 882/2004.

Equidae which are issued a duplicate or replacement identification document are not excluded from the food chain contrary to the requirements of Articles 29(2)(c) and 32(2)(c) of Regulation 2015/262. Identification verification (Transponder)

Duplicate identification documents or the identification documents issued to horses older than 12 months (mentioned in paragraphs 26, 27 and 28 above) did not have the section on administration of veterinary medicinal products completed.

These do not contain all the required information and are frequently issued with no regard to the lifetime treatment of horses with veterinary medicinal products or the animals' age. Together with incomplete FCI, this results in ineligible animals entering the food chain. Additionally, late identification results in an unknown number of horses not being tested for EIA in accordance with national surveillance programme requirements.

recommendations.text: The Competent Authorities should ensure effective cooperation between their services to improve the accuracy of the data held in the national database for equidae. In particular, to ensure the database includes information when animals must be excluded from entering the food chain. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 article 4(3). Recommendation based on conclusion No. 47. Associated findings Nos. 18, 33, 36, 38 & 40.

citations.text: ANZ stated they did not have the technical knowledge to complete the administration of veterinary medicinal products section when issuing duplicate / replacement identification documents. They considered this a responsibility of NSVFSA but no mechanism exists to notify NSVFSA when duplicate / replacement identification documents are issued. Consequently, duplicate equine identification documents issued by ANZ do not have the section on administration of veterinary medicinal products completed. This lack of coordination between NSVFSA and ANZ is not in compliance with Article 4(3) of Regulation 882/2004.

The audit team reviewed database entries for the approved holding visited. One horse had been identified the previous week and was issued with a passport for the first time at 5 years of age. Consequently, it could not have been tested for EIA in previous years as required by the annual surveillance programme. A second horse had been re-identified, also the previous week, and issued a duplicate passport. CAs confirmed it is not possible to record in the database that equidae are not intended for slaughter for human consumption contrary to Article 38(1)(l) of Regulation 2015/262. The remaining information, relating to equidae checked by audit team, was correctly recorded in the database as required by Article 38(1) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262.

Order 29 of 2014 requires an annual census of all bovine, ovine, caprine and porcine species by NSVFSA. This is carried out by free practicing veterinarians on behalf of CSVFSA. During this census, a count is taken of the number of equidae present. NSVFSA confirmed that during the census on each holding, free practicing veterinarians do not use the previous year's census or information recorded on ANZ database as a reference for the number of equidae present on a particular holding. In counties visited, CSVFSA establish a new set of records for each census2. 7

Equidae sent for rendering are accompanied, inter alia, by a sanitary veterinary certificate issued by free practicing veterinarians. This certificate includes consignor and consignee details and transponder number. On a monthly basis, free practicing veterinarians report all mortalities to CSVFSA. This data is reported on a quarterly basis to NSVFSA who confirmed they did not share this information with ANZ. No other source exists to supply this information to ANZ.

Information on the number of live equidae registered in Romania varied significantly between CAs. In one county visited by audit team, CSVFSA recorded a horse population of approximately 5500 equidae in contrast to 9951 recorded on ANZ database (as of 14 April 2016). At a national level, in 2015, ANZ equine database recorded 762 760 animals while NSVFSA recorded 455 614 equidae. CAs confirmed there is currently no collaboration between them to address this inconsistency. Enforcement

The absence of cooperation and coordination between ANZ and NSVFSA leads to duplication of efforts and data regarding horses and to uncertainty on the reliability of most data and statistics regarding equidae. The opportunities missed to share and update data restricts their usefulness for disease control purposes.

recommendations.text: NSVFSA should ensure that a system is in place to ensure that when a transponder cannot be recovered from the body of an equine animal slaughtered for human consumption the meat or part of meat containing transponder is declared unfit for human consumption. Article 34(3) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. Recommendation based on conclusion No.49. Associated findings No. 31.

citations.text: NSVFSA confirmed there was no written procedure when transponder could not be recovered from the body of an animal slaughtered for human consumption. The OV confirmed that in such a case, carcase would be passed as fit for human consumption with no treatment of the meat or part of the meat containing the transponder as unfit for human consumption. This is not in compliance with Article 34(3) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262.

The lack of instruction and / or training to deal with non-recovered transponders has caused unfit meat to enter the human food chain. 9 5.2 SUPPORT FOR ANIMAL HEALTH CONTROLS, TRADE AND IMPORTATION OF EQUIDAE Legal requirements Commission Decision 2010/346/EU on protective measures with regard to equine infectious anaemia in Romania. Findings

recommendations.text: All relevant food chain information must be made available for equidae presented for slaughter. This should be verified by CA as required by Article 4(2) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion No.45. Associated findings No.25.

citations.text: For all three equidae, FCI was not completed at section 3.4 meaning there was no attestation that withdrawal periods, for any veterinary medicines administered over the previous month, had been respected. CA agreed FCI was incomplete. A further five FCI documents from the previous weeks slaughter were reviewed. In three FCI documents (covering 46 horses) section 3.4 had not been completed. Official controls allowed these 46 animals to proceed for slaughter for human consumption. The incomplete FCI is not in compliance with Section III to Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

Weaknesses exist in the system to issue equine identification documents. These do not contain all the required information and are frequently issued with no regard to the lifetime treatment of horses with veterinary medicinal products or the animals' age. Together with incomplete FCI, this results in ineligible animals entering the food chain. Additionally, late identification results in an unknown number of horses not being tested for EIA in accordance with national surveillance programme requirements.

recommendations.text: The Competent Authorities should ensure that equine identification documents are of the correct format and content. Article 7(2) and 7(3) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 45. Associated findings Nos. 9, 10 & 52.

citations.text: Horses for breeding and production are issued with a pre-printed identification document. The free practicing veterinarian implants a transponder and completes the outline diagram. This document is then sent to ANZ or, for free practicing veterinarians with access to the ANZ database, uploaded. In all cases, the drawing must be sent in hard copy to ANZ. A pre-printed identification document is then issued. The requirement to include a section for the suspension / revalidation of the identification 3 document for movement of equidae is not included in the pre-printed identification document contrary to Article 7(2)(b) of Regulation 2015/262.

These pre-printed identification documents are currently issued with the section on administration of veterinary medicinal products stapled to the main document as an addendum. The audit team reviewed 20 identification documents returned to two county ANZ offices from slaughterhouses. Examples were seen of this single page being stamped to show association with passport, the single page being cut into separate sections with no attempt to link (stamp) these separate sections to the main passport and the section on administration of veterinary medicinal products being absent. This is not in compliance with Article 7(2)(b) of Regulation 2015/262. Furthermore, the requirement for the passport to be indivisible is not met as required by part 2(c) of Annex I of Regulation 2015/262.

Weaknesses exist in the system to issue equine identification documents. These do not contain all the required information and are frequently issued with no regard to the lifetime treatment of horses with veterinary medicinal products or the animals' age. Together with incomplete FCI, this results in ineligible animals entering the food chain. Additionally, late identification results in an unknown number of horses not being tested for EIA in accordance with national surveillance programme requirements.

The audit team reviewed the identification document relating to a horse for breeding and production, with a positive EIA test result. EIA was confirmed in March 2013 and the animal slaughtered in March 2015. The identification document correctly recorded the positive test result as required by Annex I, Part 1 of Regulation 2015/262. However, movement restrictions applied to this animal could not be recorded as the identification document did not include section III (see (9) above). NSVFSA confirmed that a lack of funding for EIA eradication during the period 2006 ­ 2007 reduced confidence in the compensation process and made some owners reluctant to release their animals for slaughter. Since 2009, the funds for compensation are allocated by the NSVFSA.

audits.title: National audit system

recommendations.text: To apply a risk-based approach in the development of the audit programme in order to meet the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and the specific 2. requirement of Article 3 of said Regulation. 3. Recommendation based on conclusion: 38 Associated findings: 26, 33 and 34 To ensure that the audit process is subject to independent scrutiny as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 19 Associated finding: 18 To ensure that the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development fulfils its obligations under Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 10 Associated finding: 7 27

citations.text: The audit procedure developed by the TAS (Code PS-01-DATC) sets out how to develop the multi-annual / annual audit programme. The main criteria taken into account for its development are as follows: - the areas of NSVFSA competence (the competent authority has defined 33 areas of official controls but this list does not appear in the audit-related procedures) 12 - the results of internal and external audits conducted in previous years - changes in legislation - changes in the organisation of structures involved in the control systems - the national and international epidemiological situation in the area of animal health - the evolution of various animal diseases - NSVFSA policies on the eradication of certain animal diseases - the results of the implementation of the MANCP - the number and size of farms, food establishments, and statistical data on production, imports etc. - rapid alert system for food and feed (RASFF) notifications (this criterion is included in the audit procedure but is not currently used as input for the audit programming ­ the Audit Directorate stated that it would be used in the future) - new scientific data, risk assessments. Whilst the procedure is clear, there are gaps in the way the TAS documents the steps it takes to justify how it draws up the programme using the procedure. Based on the TAS representatives' statements, they partially use the procedure but they do not clearly record how they arrive from the plan to the presentation of the audit programme.

Whilst the audit universe has been defined (albeit not well-documented), the risk universe has not. Out of the 33 areas identified in the audit universe, 16 of these are related to specific animal health issues, two are related to animal welfare issues, and the remaining 15 cover very broad categories such as border inspection posts, food hygiene under Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, poultry meat and derivatives thereof, etc. When the official control areas have not been subject to a detailed breakdown, as is the case with all the areas identified in the audit universe excepting animal health, it is difficult to properly define the risks, as different aspects (e.g. product, process, establishment type etc.) will present a different level of risk. Furthermore, there is no methodology in place to assign a risk ranking to each aspect. For example, in the case of food hygiene, the TAS did not break this area down into official controls in different types of establishment (mobile food sellers, restaurants, primary production, processing plants, wholesalers, retailers, mass catering etc.), size of establishment/volume of production, production processes etc. In the example given, the TAS could not therefore justify why official controls in slaughterhouses, for example, were considered a higher risk than those in restaurants.

The TAS had planned to audit some areas more than once in the five year audit programme cycle but could not demonstrate why some areas were prioritised over others, except for the ad-hoc audits ordered by the President of the NSVFSA. The concept of 'adequate coverage of all relevant areas of activity' of point 5.1 of Decision 2006/677/EC was taken to mean 'audit' of all relevant areas, rather than risk-based consideration of all relevant areas. 14

The approach to risk-based planning is inadequately documented and defined. There is no recorded risk analysis methodology to describe the areas in sufficient detail, and the relevant process is not documented or transparent. Therefore, the TAS could not demonstrate the risk basis for the frequency of auditing some areas nor justify the exclusion of other areas.

audits.title: PDO, PGI and TSG of Agricultural Products and Foodstuffs and Geographical Indications (GI) of spirit drinks

recommendations.text: Ensure that the CAs delegating specific tasks to CBs organise audits or inspections as necessary in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 15 Associated findings Nos 11, 13, 14.

citations.text: The CA confirmed that they do not undertake any shadow audits of the CB inspectors as part of their supervisory activities. A representative of MARD may occasionally attend the RENAR accreditation audit of a CB as an observer. An accreditation audit occurs once every four years for each CB. However, as no judgement is made by the CA in these observation roles, it cannot be considered to be part of the supervisory activity of the CB. 5

The audit team reviewed a number of the reports prepared by the CA relating to the CB office audits. These mainly describe the findings that the CBs have observed during producers/processor inspections during the previous year. However, the CA does not evaluate the activities of the CB.

The fact that the CA does not carry out any witness audits of the CB inspectors at the operator level does not permit the CA to evaluate the effectiveness of inspections carried out by CBs. This lack of supervisory activities by the CA is not in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted some systematic shortcomings in the inspections carried out by the CBs (see paras 33, 34 and 35). Such shortcoming could only be detected through carrying out such witness inspections. Conclusions on Control Bodies

The CA delegates certain official control tasks to CBs which are accredited to ISO17065. Supervision of the CBs by the CA is not fully effective as the supervisory process does not include witness inspections, which is not in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 22(1) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls are carried out without prior warning as required by Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 23, 38 Associated findings Nos 16,26

citations.text: Given the relatively small number of producers/processors of PDO/PGI agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks in Romania the approach taken has been to subject all producers/processors to an annual official control. At the time of the audit the official controls for agriproducts and foodstuffs were delegated to CBs whereas official controls of spirit drinks were undertaken by the CA. The CCA confirmed that all annual official controls at producers/processor level for both types of registered names are announced. 6 This is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which states that official controls shall be carried out without prior warning.

All annual official controls of producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks are announced which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004

The audit team visited two producers of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and three producers of GI spirit drinks. In all cases, a series of inspection reports were available which illustrated that all producers/processors were subject to an annual official control. The audit team was informed that all inspections at operators whether carried out by CAs (spirit drinks) or CBs (agriproducts and foodstuffs) are announced. The CA stated that this approach ensured that inspections take place at the time of processing and that all relevant documents are prepared by the operators. 8 Agriproducts and Foodstuffs ­ Controls Undertaken by CBs

Although official controls are undertaken at an agreed frequency at producers/processors, the inspections are announced, superficial and do not always include each element of the Product Specification/Technical Files. Consequently, this approach does not provide the necessary level of assurance that producers/processors are fully compliant. 5.2.6 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that routine risk based market controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks protected in the EU are included in the prioritisation of official controls as required by Article 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 25 Associated findings Nos 19, 21

citations.text: At the time of the audit, there were no risk based market controls in place which is not in line with Article 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Verification of compliance with product specification and specifications in the technical file prior to placing a product on the market

At the time of the audit, the CA confirmed that there were no risk based market controls in place in Romania. However, the NACP undertakes investigations of ad-hoc consumer complaints as they arise. A number of case studies were described by the NACP which illustrated their competence to investigate and to sanction where appropriate. One complicated investigation related to a registered name from a non-EU country. The NACP had received a complaint that coffee which was not the genuine article had been traded in Romania. The NACP successfully identified the source of the problem and implemented the relevant enforcement measures. 7 Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls

Routine risk based market controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks were not included in the prioritisation of official controls at the time of the audit. 5.2.4 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 664/2014, in particular Article 1. Commission implementing Regulation (EU) No 668/2014, in particular Article 4. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Articles 8(1), 9 and 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011. Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Findings Controls at Visited Premises

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls at producers/processors include the verification of every element of the Product Specification/Technical Files as required by Article 37 of Regulation (EU) No1151/2012 and Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Recommendation is based on conclusion Nos 24, 38 Associated findings Nos 18,28, 34

citations.text: In relation to spirit drinks, the annual official control at producers/processors did not include the checking of all elements of the technical file and neither did it include, sampling, for laboratory analysis. This could not ensure compliance with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008.
The lack of official sampling and laboratory analysis of spirit drinks means that the requirements of Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 are not met.

It was noted that raw materials were accepted on the basis of a general declaration by the supplier, that the raw materials complied with the requirements of the Product Specification. As an example, the CB never raised a non-compliance regarding the absence of labelling of a specific raw material. This acceptance signifies a lack of control measures.

In the spirit drink producers visited, although the operators kept records as regards the production, as well as purchase and sales records, no verification of the information in these were made by the inspectors. The inspectors stated that such controls were undertaken by the revenue authorities. 9

Although official controls are undertaken at an agreed frequency at producers/processors, the inspections are announced, superficial and do not always include each element of the Product Specification/Technical Files. Consequently, this approach does not provide the necessary level of assurance that producers/processors are fully compliant. 5.2.6 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. audits.title: Animal Health - African Swine Fever

recommendations.text: To immediately start testing samples of dead pigs from industrial commercial pig holdings for ASF (which are submitted to laboratory under passive surveillance for classical swine fever) to ensure that passive surveillance covers the entire domestic pig population and meets the objectives of the approved programme i.e. monitoring and early detection of the presence of ASF virus in the susceptible population of domestic pigs. Approved programme for ASF (2016 ­ 2018). Recommendation based on conclusion No. 54. Associated finding Nos. 35, 37, 39 and 41.

citations.text: The current multi-annual programme requires sampling and laboratory analysis of domestic pigs found sick or dead, from non-commercial holdings across the entire territory of Romania, where classical and ASF could not be ruled out (passive surveillance). This surveillance does not apply to commercial holdings.

In two industrial commercial farms visited by the audit team, the private veterinarians providing a service had both submitted in 2016, pig carcases to regional laboratories for post mortem examination. In both cases the veterinarian had requested classical swine fever testing but not ASF testing. The authorities confirmed that samples submitted for classical swine fever testing were paid by the authorities but ASF analysis in commercial industrial farms had to be paid by farmer. In contrast, backyard holdings do not have to pay for ASF testing.

The competent authority provided results of passive surveillance in domestic pigs: County 2015 2016 Botosani 0 58 Galati 14 140 Iasi 23 24 Maramures 40 74 Satu Mare 0 103 Suceava 22 126 Vaslui 20 43 Tulcea 33 62 Total 630 152

The number of passive surveillance samples taken has increased between 2015 and 2016. In the counties visited, the audit team confirmed that the majority of these samples were from non-commercial holdings. 10

Should the disease enter the domestic pig population, passive surveillance is more likely to detect it early in backyard holdings, while in commercial holdings, detection will be probably delayed due to the absence of passive surveillance. The existing long laboratory turnaround times hamper early detection and if they persist once the disease is detected, these will create difficulties in the containment of disease. 5.3 EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS FOR ASF Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 8, 21, 22, Annex VI of Dir. 2002/60, Dec. 2003/422, Dir.92/119 12 Findings 5.3.1 National plan and operations manual

recommendations.text: Practical arrangements should be put in place to increase the number of dead wild boar reported in the eight at risk counties in order to meet the objectives of the approved programme i.e. monitoring and early detection of the presence of ASF virus in the susceptible population of wild boars. Approved programme for ASF (2016 ­ 2018). Recommendation based on conclusion No. 52. Associated finding Nos. 24, 25, 26, and 29.

citations.text: The current multi-annual programme (2016 - 2018) for the surveillance and control of ASF requires sampling and laboratory analysis of all wild boar found dead or sick and those killed in road traffic accidents from the entire territory of Romania (passive surveillance). In normal conditions it is expected that the minimum number of wild boar to be found in a given area is ~ 1% of wild boar population at risk. Based on this, the minimum number of wild boar sampled in the eight at risk counties in 2016 should have been ~170 (Total wild boar population was 17021). Additionally, in the eight at risk counties, the programme requires sampling and analysis (by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)) for ASF in all hunted wild boar (active surveillance). The competent authority provided numbers of wild boar sampled under active and passive surveillance, in the eight at risk counties: 2015 2016 County Active Passive Active Passive surveillance surveillance surveillance surveillance Botosani Galati 60 0 355 2 Iasi Maramures 140 21 211 10 Satu Mare Suceava 306 0 414 3 Vaslui Tulcea 551 0 738 12 TOTAL 580 0 848 3 339 0 455 4 55 0 271 2 103 0 128 0 2,134 21 3,420 36 8 Passive surveillance

Finding dead wild boars is a challenge due to the large numbers of natural predators, cannibalism by the wild boar themselves and the tendency for dying wild boar to seek secluded areas where it is difficult to find them. Currently, there are no incentives encouraging hunters to overcome this challenge, on the contrary (a) hunters are expected to transport found dead wild boar to the nearest laboratory at their own expense and (b) hunters lose one animal from their hunting bag for each found dead wild boar reported.

The competent authority plans to incentivise reporting of found dead wild boar but cannot implement financial incentives until the budget is approved in line with National Decision 1156/2013 which lays down the budget for all animal disease control in Romania. They indicated this would take at least 60 days.

In 2015, Romania collected a low number of passive surveillance samples - all from one county. In 2016, the situation improved slightly with most at risk counties submitting samples. The numbers of samples submitted is well below the estimates for meaningful passive surveillance and early detection of disease. Active surveillance

The current surveillance programme on wild boars, in particular the poor passive surveillance, does not provide confidence that ASF would be detected at an early stage following introduction. This will delay the detection of the disease and thus the implementation of control measures, increasing the risk for further spread into domestic pigs, particularly into backyard holdings.

recommendations.text: The turnaround time for submitting, testing and reporting laboratory results for samples submitted under passive surveillance for ASF should be shortened to meet the objectives of the approved programme for early detection of ASF virus. This should include a mechanism for prioritising samples where ASF cannot be ruled out. Approved programme for ASF (2016 ­ 2018). Recommendation based on conclusion No. 54. Associated finding Nos. 49 and 50. 17

citations.text: Only domestic pigs from non-commercial holdings, submitted to regional laboratories for classical swine fever passive surveillance, are routinely tested for ASF. When at 2 King et al, 2003 3 Fernandez-Pinero et al, 2013 11 regional level, a sample tests negative to classical swine fever, the samples are then sent to the NRL for ASF testing. The audit team reviewed laboratory reports in Iasi. The interval between initial submission of samples to the laboratory network and reporting of results was up to one month ­ despite haemorrhagic lesions being identified at post- mortem examination in regional laboratory. This does not meet the objectives of the approved programme for early detection of ASF.

The audit team reviewed the 2017 laboratory reports in Satu Mare for passive surveillance in domestic pigs. They showed delays in submission of samples from the regional laboratory to the NRL of up to two weeks. Results of ASF testing were available on the laboratory information management system within two days of receipt by the NRL, but it took another ten days before regional staff became aware of these results.

Should the disease enter the domestic pig population, passive surveillance is more likely to detect it early in backyard holdings, while in commercial holdings, detection will be probably delayed due to the absence of passive surveillance. The existing long laboratory turnaround times hamper early detection and if they persist once the disease is detected, these will create difficulties in the containment of disease. 5.3 EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS FOR ASF Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 8, 21, 22, Annex VI of Dir. 2002/60, Dec. 2003/422, Dir.92/119 12 Findings 5.3.1 National plan and operations manual

recommendations.text: To enforce the requirement for an up-to-date register of movements (including the date, the origin or the destination, and the identification marks) to strengthen traceability in backyard and type A holdings. Article 4(1) of Directive 2008/71/EC; Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 70. Associated finding Nos. 66 and 67.

citations.text: None of the four backyard or commercial type A holdings visited by the audit team had an up-to-date register of movements, which is not in line with Article 4(1) of Directive 2008/71/EC ­ this issue was previously identified in DG(SANCO)2014-7045. In contrast, the two industrial commercial farms visited had comprehensive records available showing e.g. movements, daily mortalities and the number and weight of dead pigs sent for rendering.

Circumscription veterinarians perform an annual census on all holdings which includes pigs. If the database has pigs recorded as being present on a holding but the animals are not in the farm when the annual census is done, the circumscription veterinarian moves these animals to a virtual holding ­ named RO0000000000. The authorities confirmed that in 2016, the number of pigs that moved into virtual holding was 1,302,501. 5.3.3 Simulation exercises

Although identification and movement controls for pigs go generally beyond EU legal requirements, the absence of records such as holding registers, geographic co-ordinates and field for sanitary information together with the large numbers of backyard pigs moving to a "virtual holding" (i.e. with an unknown destination) will significantly weaken the tracing of pigs and containment of disease in an outbreak scenario. 5.4 VERIFICATION, SUPERVISION AND EXPERT GROUP Legal requirements Articles 4 and 8 of Regulation No 882/2004; Directive 2002/60/EC (Articles 15, 16 and 22, Annex VI) Findings 5.4.1. Supervision by line management

recommendations.text: Collaboration between NSVFSA and the Ministry of Water & Forestry should be strengthened at central and county level to ensure wild boar populations are managed to reach (and maintain) a low wild boar density through e.g. implementation of a total feed ban and targeted hunting of females. SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 4 ­ ASF Strategy for Eastern Part of the EU. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 19. Associated finding Nos. 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10.

citations.text: Six out of the eight counties at risk have wild boar densities between 0.25 ­ 0.5 / km². The two remaining counties have wild boar densities between 0.5 ­ 0.75 / km² (see map below). The current ASF strategy for the eastern part of the EU considers a wild boar density of 0.5 wild boar / km² or lower as optimal to reduce the spread of ASF.

Wild boar densities are calculated on the total surface area of a county rather than the area of suitable biotype for wild boar (forest and agricultural land) within the county. Consequently, this does not reflect the true density.
Trends for national wild boar populations provided by competent authorities demonstrate a year on year increase in the wild boar population (see graph). EVOLUTION OF WILD BOARS POPULATION ­ 2008-2015

County representatives of the Ministry of Water and Forestry record census results for each individual hunting ground. The audit team reviewed detailed records in one county visited showing actual and optimum wild boar densities (calculated by the Ministry of 4 Water and Forestry) by individual hunting ground and data relating to hunting quotas approved and actually achieved. In all 55 hunting grounds in one county, the actual number of wild boar exceeded the optimal number calculated for the particular biotype. For the period reviewed, 2015 and 2016, wild boar numbers were shown to increase.

National legislation (Decision No. 830 of 9 November 2016) approves the national programme for the surveillance, prevention and control of ASF in the country. Article 28 applies to wild boar populations and includes e.g. prohibiting feeding of wild boars and selective hunting of females aimed at achieving a wild boar density of < 0.5 / km². The competent authority confirmed that these measures will only be applied on confirmation of the first case of ASF.

The existing contracts between the Ministry of Water and Forestry and hunting ground managers are contributing to a year on year increase in the wild boar population with no evidence of arrangements in place between Ministry of Water and Forestry and the NSVFSA to reverse this trend. This increasing population will favour the spread of ASF and create difficulties in its elimination and control should the disease reach Romania.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the national database for animals, SNIIA, contains all required information including the geographic co-ordinates of all registered pig holdings and a field where sanitary information can be recorded. Article 1 (1)(d) and 1(1)(e) to Commission Decision 2000/678/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 70. Associated finding Nos. 59 and 60.

citations.text: Competent authorities confirmed that the national database for animals, SNIIA, does not contain a complete record of geographic co-ordinates for all registered pig holdings as required by Article 1 (1)(d) to Commission Decision 2000/678/EC.

The database does not have a field where the competent authority could enter sanitary information, which is not in line with Article 1(e) to Commission Decision 2000/678/EC. Consequently, the database cannot be used for implementation and verification of ASF movement restrictions.

Although identification and movement controls for pigs go generally beyond EU legal requirements, the absence of records such as holding registers, geographic co-ordinates and field for sanitary information together with the large numbers of backyard pigs moving to a "virtual holding" (i.e. with an unknown destination) will significantly weaken the tracing of pigs and containment of disease in an outbreak scenario. 5.4 VERIFICATION, SUPERVISION AND EXPERT GROUP Legal requirements Articles 4 and 8 of Regulation No 882/2004; Directive 2002/60/EC (Articles 15, 16 and 22, Annex VI) Findings 5.4.1. Supervision by line management

recommendations.text: Ensure that, in cooperation with County Prefect, competent authorities have plans in place for the disposal of animals following depopulation when rendering is not an option.

audits.title: Import control system (live animals, food of animal and non-animal origin)

recommendations.text: To ensure that the BIP facilities are maintained and equipped in compliance with the requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC and Directive 91/496/EEC. Recommendation based on conclusion:70 Associated findings: 54, 55, 56, 60, 64, 66, 67, 68 and 69

citations.text: However, the facilities were not well-maintained (flaking paint in the unloading area for products of human consumption due to an old leak and a damaged unloading ramp) and equipment unrelated to the performance of import controls was kept in the facilities.

In addition, the facilities were used for purposes other than those intended e.g. storage facilities at ambient temperature were used to store office supplies. In the facilities rodent pellets for pest control were exposed.

The fridge in the inspection room for products of human consumption contained meat which could not be traced to its original consignment. The content of another fridge, although in operation, could not be inspected by the audit team as the BIP staff claimed not to have a key. 5.3.2 Albia

The facilities and equipment for import controls of live animals ­ categories "U and E" could be fit for purpose and brought into line with the requirements of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC on the condition that the ANSVSA installs appropriate facilities for feed and water supply. The BIP staff stated that for the two recent consignments of re-imported live pigs an ad hoc solution was applied due to the absence of appropriate feed and water facilities.

The facilities and equipment are fit for purpose. Regarding the BIPs, these are in line with the requirements of Annex II to Directive 97/78/EC and the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC, and regarding DPEs, these are in line with the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009. However, the facilities were not kept clean (overhead dust and old spider webs) and equipment unrelated to the performance of import controls was kept in the facilities. 5.3.4 Halmeu

The facilities and equipment were not entirely fit for their purpose. Regarding the BIPs, these are in not in line with the requirements of Annex II to Directive 97/78/EC and the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC, and regarding DPEs, these are not in line with the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009. The facilities were not kept clean (overhead dust and old spider webs) and had not been maintained following some leaks. In addition, equipment unrelated to the performance of import controls was kept in the inspection room.
The storage facilities for chilled, frozen and ambient products have not been used for the storage of products since the approval of the BIP in 2006, but were kept clean and maintained.
The facilities for live animals were not well-maintained and leaks had caused damage to the walls and floors.

The storage facilities for animal-by-products were not in operation, due to a breakdown in the electricity supply. These products were temporarily stored in a freezer kept in the unloading area for live ungulates and equidae. Conclusions on the suitability of facilities

The facilities, equipment and hygiene of the BIPs/DPEs visited, were in general adequate for undertaking controls on imports though permanent solutions are needed for the feeding and watering facilities for the live animal categories "U and E" in the BIP Albia and for facilities' maintenance in the BIPs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The organisation of the competent authorities and their functional responsibilities changed in June 2018. Since then BIPs/DPEs/DPIs are under the direct responsibility of the County 13 Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Directorates instead of the central authority level (although in reality there have been no consignments destined for DPIs for several years). It is too early to gauge the impact of this change on the effectiveness of the control system for imports, nevertheless, the audit team considers that the framework in which official controls on imports are conducted is adequate, being supported by documented procedures, information technology systems and relevant training for staff. This framework contributes to efficient coordination and cooperation within and between the various designated competent authorities, effective planning and consistent implementation of controls on imports. The central authority has verified and documented in detail the performance of BIPs/DPEs in recent years (prior to the reattribution of responsibilities). The audit team considered that this had contributed to improvements in official import controls. Implementation of official controls on imported live animals and products of both animal and non-animal origin was generally in line with EU legislation; the provisions of special import conditions on certain products of plant origin were implemented as required. There is an appropriate annual monitoring plan for imported food and feed in place, with the objective of detecting potential hazards to humans, animals and the environment. The audit team identified a number of issues with the conduct of controls which can easily be corrected by amending the staff instructions. The central authority committed to doing this. Regarding the facilities, equipment and hygiene of the BIPs/DPEs visited, these were in general adequate for undertaking controls on imports though permanent solutions are needed for the feeding and watering facilities for the live animal categories "U and E" in the BIP Albia and for maintenance of facilities in the BIPs visited. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 16 October 2018 with the representatives of the ANSVSA and Customs. At this meeting, the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. The ANSVSA did not express disagreement with the findings and conclusions presented and provided some clarifications. The ANSVSA stated that a procedure to handle waste as a result of official controls was being developed and would be signed as soon as possible. The audit team received a copy of the approved procedure shortly after completion of the audit. 14 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. No. Recommendation 1. To ensure that the BIP facilities are maintained and equipped in compliance with the requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC and Directive 91/496/EEC. Recommendation based on conclusion:70 Associated findings: 54, 55, 56, 60, 64, 66, 67, 68 and 69 The competent authority's response to the recommendations can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/rep_details_en.cfm?rep_inspection_ref=2018-6320 15 ANNEX 1 ­ LEGAL REFERENCES Legal Reference Official Journal Title Reg. 2658/87 OJ L 256, 7.9.1987, Council Regulation (EEC) No 2658/87 of 23 p. 1-675 July 1987 on the tariff and statistical nomenclature and on the Common Customs Tariff Reg. 178/2002 OJ L 3

Deadline: 30.06.2019 County Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Authority Constanta BIP North Constanta: - The hygiene of the premises of the BIP will be provided by the cleaning company with which the DSVSA has a contract. recommendations.text: Ensure that national legislation on organic production is fully in line with Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Recommendation based on conclusion 3 Associated finding 2

citations.text: Based on a review of this legislation, the audit team noted that some provisions contained in Article 9 of Ministerial Order No 895/2016 are not fully in line with Articles 65(4) and 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Article 9 of Ministerial Order No 895/2016 stipulates that the CBs must carry out additional random unannounced visits to at least 10% of operators under contract (Article 92c(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 stipulates that 10% of the total inspections carried out by the CB must be unannounced). recommendations.text: Ensure that the exchange of information between CBs in cases where an operator changes their control body includes all relevant elements of the control file of the operator concerned in accordance with Article 92(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and the reports referred in Article 63(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Recommendation based on conclusion 15 Associated finding 13

citations.text: The CBs have procedures in place for certification of operators who move between CBs. The audit team reviewed one file related to transfer of operators and noted that not all relevant information related to the operators concerned was exchanged between the CBs involved. The CB just informed the other CB that the relevant operator had irregularities and was no longer covered by that CB as the certification was not renewed. This is not in line with Article 92(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which requires that the previous CB must hand over all the relevant elements of the control file and reports referred in Article 63(2) to the subsequent CB.

A system of control is in place in accordance with EU provisions. CAs are designated with a clear division of responsibilities and tasks between CAs and CBs. There is good communication between the CAs and the CBs and other involved parties which includes the regular exchange of relevant information on the results of controls. Recommendation based on conclusion 45 Associated findings 40, 42 and 43

citations.text: The CB plan additional inspections and sampling of organic operators based on a risk assessment. The CB visited uses criteria to classify operators into high, medium and low risk categories. Different criteria to classify operators are used depending on the type of activity carried out by the operator (primary production, processor, importer etc.) which include inter alia previous non-compliances, the size of the business, the risk for exchange of products or the complexity and type of activities. The CB has a complex system for the classification of operators using a number of criteria allocating score points to each criterion using a formula. However, the criterion for risk assessment does not include the quantity produced which is not in line with Article 65 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

According to the CB's procedure, all operators classified in high risk and 80% of operators classified in medium risk must be selected for additional visits. If necessary, low risk operators are included to complete the 10% of additional visits. However, the audit team noted that the selection of operators for additional visits for 2017 was not in line with the described procedures. Only 47% of high risk operators were visited and around 60% of medium risk were visited (specifically 18 of additional audits took place in high risk operators, 238 in medium risk operators and 144 in low risk operators). A significant number of low risk operators were also selected for additional visits. The CB stated that all high risk operators which could not be visited in 2017 were visited at the beginning of 2018. This is not fully in line with Article 92c(2)(a) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 899/2008. 10

The CB sampling is based on the risk assessment made to select operators for additional visits (see paragraph 40). According to the CB's procedure, 100% of high risk operators and 50% of medium risk operators should be selected for sampling. If necessary, low risk operators are selected to reach the minimum 5% stipulated in the legislation. However, in 2017 the CB did not fully follow its procedure for the selection of operators from sampling as 10 low risk operators were sampled while not 100% of high risk operators and 50% of medium risk operators were subject for sampling. Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls

However, the effectiveness of the system is reduced as there is a risk that not all the highest risk operators are selected for additional inspections and sampling as the CB visited did not fully follow its own procedure for selecting operators based on the level of risk and the quantity produced is not taken into account as a criterion for risk assessment.

citations.text: In one case, a major non-compliance was notified by the parent company of the CB located in another MS. In this case, one Romanian operator imported two batches of plums from non-EU countries (the 1st, 20 tonnes of plums from Moldova and the 2nd, 20 tonnes of plums from Serbia) and both were found contaminated with PPPs (cypermethrine and pyrimethanil). The samples were taken from a client of the Romanian operator in France. Both batches were directly transferred from the non-EU countries to France; the role of Romanian operator was to make the arrangements for the import of the products. The CB in Romania was notified about the results of the laboratory analyses that took place in France on 17/08/2016. After that, the Romanian CB carried out an inspection of the Romanian operator and discovered that the two batches had entered the EU market without a certificate of inspection. The CB decided to suspend the activity of the operator on 8/12/2016 and notified the CCA on 9/12/2016. The CB finally decided to withdraw the certificate of the operator on 3/3/2017 but the operator was afterward registered with another CB which is not in line with Article 19(14) of Order 895/2016 (i.e. an operator who has been excluded from the organic farming system is not entitled to register in the organic farming system for a period of five years from the date of exclusion). In addition, the CCA did not notify the case to OFIS as is required in Article 92a(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

The CCA failed to ensure that de-certified operators are excluded from the organic system for a period of five years in line with national legislation.

citations.text: During the recent potato crop production periods, the NPA and its regional county offices had not organised information campaigns, conferences or any other events on potato bacteria. Extension and/or consultation services to producers or other operators of the potato production and marketing sectors are provided occasionally at the beginning of the potato surveillance period or after ring rot outbreaks.

Non-registered growers usually state that they do not grow potatoes for commercial purposes but only for their own needs or limited local circulation (family consumption or animal feed). According to the data provided, in 2017 there were 49,125 small scale and 5,547 larger scale (more than one ha) producers who were receiving subsidies from 7 the APIA but were not registered with the NPA. This is not in line with the national requirement for registration with the NPA of potato producers with more than 0.5 ha and Article 6.6 of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The audit team came across cases of small scale non-professional producers growing potatoes on more than 0.5 ha who, despite being registered with APIA, stated that they were not aware of the obligatory registration with the NPA or that, in any case, they could not afford the registration fees imposed by the NPA.

Data from the National Statistics Service of Romania indicate that during 2017 ca. 133,600 ha were cultivated with ware potatoes. However, despite a collaboration agreement between the NPA and APIA, there is no consistent access by the NPA to the database of APIA. The producers with ware potato areas totaling more than 0.5 ha who do not comply with the requirement of registration in the phytosanitary database are not known by the NPA. Overall, producers registered with the NPA correspond only to ca. 9.5% of the total ware potato producing area; the majority (ca. 70%) of the area of ware potatoes is grown by operators who are not registered either with the NPA or APIA. Conclusion on organisational aspects of plant health controls

However, only limited awareness raising efforts regarding ring rot and brown rot have been made by the regional competent authorities to inform potato producers. These do not cover adequately the registration requirements when moving or trading potatoes. Despite the legal obligation for their registration with the NPA, registration of producers is not enforced. A large number of producers remain unregistered, and hence, they are not subject to supervision or systematic controls.

As there is lack of communication functionality between the databases of the NPA and the APIA, compliance with phytosanitary registration requirements cannot be verified against the APIA database. This reduces the capacity of the NPA to have a proper overview and control of the current ring rot situation. The consequences of this are compounded by the fact that a very large proportion of the subsidised potato production in Romania is produced from non-tested farm saved material of unknown origin and health status. 8 5.2 CONTROL OF CLAVIBACTER MICHIGANENSIS SSP. SEPEDONICUS AND RALSTONIA SOLANACEARUM 5.2.1 Cms and Rs surveillance strategy and results Legal requirements Article 2 of Directive 93/85/EEC and Article 2 of Directive 98/57/EC. Findings

Despite the elaboration of the "Programme to eradicate and prevent the spread of harmful organisms Cms and Rs", there is currently no concrete target or action plan for the systematic reduction of incidence and the ultimate eradication of ring rot. However, Article 1 of Directive 93/85/EEC requires Member States to take measures in order to eradicate the disease.

At the time of the audit, Romania had not adopted any provisions to promote or subsidise the use of certified seed by producers and had not launched broad information 17 campaigns in order to inform producers on potato diseases. A memorandum had been prepared with suggestions to producers for using certified seed.

During interviews with regional plant health inspectors and potato producers the audit team also noted that: In some cases producers stated that they could not find certified potato seed for sale. In line with the current system of agricultural subsidies, certain ware potato producers might still be eligible for receiving financial support whilst still not registered with the NPA and continue to use non-certified / non-tested potato propagating material, often of unknown origin. Even large scale seed and ware potato producers and wholesalers do not apply any treatments for the preventive disinfection of potato seed transporting vehicles, agricultural machinery, storage facilities or any other farm equipment such as wooden crates in order to avoid cross contamination and spread of potato bacteria; Despite the generally widespread knowledge about the importance of following good hygiene conditions in the places of production, at national level there is no agreed hygiene protocol covering all aspects of potato production, sorting, storage, transport and processing, indicating the details on the succession and the timeframe of actions to be taken. Conclusions on the specific ring rot and brown rot control programme

There is no concrete action plan for the systematic reduction and ultimate eradication of Cms and the measures taken for its control have only temporary and limited effect. Romania has not adopted any additional measures against Cms, such as, actions to promote or subsidise the use of certified or tested seed. Deployment of a hygiene protocol for use at least in places of production of large scale professional producers, distributors and for processors has not been considered. 5.2.4 Documentation and traceability of potato consignments Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2000/29/EC. Point 18.5 of Annex IV, Part A, Section II to the same Directive. Article 3 of Directive 2002/56/EC. Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that where operators change their CB, the change is notified without delay to the CA. Recommendation based on conclusion 9 Associated finding 8

citations.text: Evidence presented by CB1 confirmed there was delayed notification to MARD and other CBs of operators who moved from CB1 to other CBs. This is not in line with Article 92(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Competent Authorities and Control Bodies

A control system is in place with clearly defined responsibilities for CAs and CBs. There is good cooperation among these players and regular reporting of control results. However, there is delayed notification of major irregularities (see also chapter 5.2.7) and of operators changing their CB. 3 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal Legal Requirements Article 5(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 27(5) to (9) and (14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92c of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that risk analysis procedures implemented by CBs are designed in a way to meet the requirement laid down in Article 92c(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Recommendation based on conclusions 17, 29 Associated findings 21, 23-25, 46

citations.text: MARD annually supervises CBs visited. Reports issued are comprehensive and clear deadlines are indicated for CBs to rectify shortcomings. However, the number of witness and review audits by MARD is low in relation to the number of operators controlled by CBs in Romania. Hence, there is a risk that relevant information is not available to the CA for its evaluation of CBs' performance. Moreover, MARD does not verify whether CBs' risk analysis procedure is fit for purpose (see chapter 5.2.3). 5.2.2 Registration of Operators Legal Requirements Article 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92(2) and 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

Both CBs visited have procedures in place for the planning and prioritisation of controls of their operators. These procedures require that all operators receive at least one annual control and that at least 10% of these operators are subject to an annual additional control based on risk evaluation. Risk criteria defined in the CBs procedures in principle include those referred to in Article 65 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

A significant weakness was noted in the risk assessment methodology used by CB1. It turned out that an operator with parallel production of annual crop having a previous major non-compliance could still be categorised as a low risk operator. This has never been contested by the MARD during its supervision of this CB.
It was also noted that the risk assessment undertaken by one individual in CB1 was not supported by documentary evidence and the approach used was considered to lack transparency and objectiveness.

Both CBs visited define the size of farms by only considering the hectares of land under organic management and leave aside the non-organically managed land. Files reviewed by the audit team confirmed that operators with land under organic management had substantially more land under non-organic management and that this situation was not taken into account for the CBs' risk assessment. CB1 classifies processors into small, medium and big operators. However, there is no quantitative measurement of what defines the CB's understanding of a small, medium and big processor in its procedures.

Both CBs visited undertake a risk assessment to prioritise controls to their operators and had fully implemented their planned controls in 2017. Both CBs exceeded by far the minimum level defined in the EU regulation for additional and unannounced controls. However, the CBs risk analysis can lead to some high risk operators being incorrectly categorised and hence not being subject to the required control frequency. 5.2.4 Controls of operators, traceability and labelling Legal Requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Article 23 and 27(13) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 65 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Title II and IV of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

Several files were reviewed by the audit team at CB2. A number of the cases related to parallel production, i.e. the growing of the same annual variety as organic and non- organic which is contrary to Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. The CB, in line with its catalogue of enforcement measures, downgraded the affected parcel and the related harvest had to be sold as non-organic which was confirmed during the following inspection. The CB confirmed that this type of non-compliance is frequently detected during on-site inspections. This CB does not require its operators to notify the annual schedule of production of crops prior to its on-site visit (as required in Article 71 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008). Consequently this information is not available for input into the risk assessment carried out by the CB. 10

recommendations.text: Ensure that documentary evidence issued by CBs comply with the model provided for in Annex XII of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and in particular include information on the non-organic activity of the operators where applicable. Recommendation based on conclusion 20 Associated finding 19

citations.text: Documentary evidence issued by the CBs visited does not contain information relating to the non-organic activity carried out by their operators. This is not in line with the model of Annex XII to Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Registration of Operators

Although there is a publicly accessible register of all organic operators, the absence of information relating to some operators' non-organic activities is a weakness. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Article 41 and Article 92f of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 5 Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 65(1) and (4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Article 92c(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure the CBs inspections are effective, as required by Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, in particular with regard to The non-organic activity of operators as provided for in Article 67(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Precautionary measures implemented by operators to reduce the risk of contamination by unauthorised products (cleaning, separation) (Article 26 and 63 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 respectively) Documentation and its appropriateness to successfully conduct traceability checks (Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC)No 889/2008) Recommendation based on conclusion 38 Associated findings 32, 34-37

citations.text: CB1 performed traceability on a selected batch of a final organic product and organic raw material stored in a warehouse. Although the CB inspectors undertook many aspects 7 of the tasks in a satisfactory manner, it took a long time for the inspectors to complete the relatively simple exercise. In addition, the inspectors were not familiar filling in the relevant forms provided by the CB.

The operator (referred to in paragraph 49) claimed that he will use the downgraded wheat for seeds in the next production season. During an unannounced inspection on 29.8.2018 CB2 noted that the above mentioned wheat was sold as non-organic. The CB verified the correctness of this action. However, the evidence was the list of harvest and the invoice with the quantities of wheat corresponding to the 2018 harvest of a parcel with 9.98 ha. There was no lot number on the invoice to establish a directly link between the product sold (type, amount) and the product harvested from the parcel in question.

CB1 inspectors appeared to be unfamiliar with the concept of critical processing steps as referred to in Article 26 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 according to which the operator shall establish and update procedures based on a systematic identification of critical processing steps and the application of these procedures shall at all times guarantee that the processed products comply with EU organic rules. Nevertheless, inspection reports reviewed by the audit team include references and description of verification of precautionary measures implemented by the operators such as cleaning measures, identification and separation. Yet some shortcomings were noted by the audit team during on-site visits:

At one processor, the raw material was delivered in bulk and stored in silos until processing took place. For the storage of the organic raw material specifically dedicated silos are used, but the same reception area for organic and non-organic raw material. CB2 interviewed the worker who was aware of the importance of cleaning between the delivery of non-organic and organic batches. As no cleaning records were available the CB inspector was unable to verify this. No measures were in place to test the effectiveness of the cleaning measures.

At the same operator, the processing of organic and the packaging of non-organic products took place at the same time and in the same room. For both products, the company used white big bags. There was no label visible on the big white bag which was about to be packaged during the presence of the audit team. The CB inspector focused checks and verification on the ongoing processing of the organic product but did not verify the non-organic activity ongoing at the same time (Article 67(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. When asked by the audit team, the CB inspector confirmed that the system of separation implemented by the company can be considered 8 sufficiently effective to reduce the risk of (accidental) mixing of organic and non- organic products. Conclusions on Controls of Operators, traceability and labelling

There is room for improvement with regard to traceability checks as well as the verification of the effectiveness of precautionary measures implemented by operators to eliminate the risk of cross-contamination between organic and non-organic products throughout the production/processing flow. 5.2.5 Sampling and laboratory analysis Legal Requirements Article 65(2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 5(2) and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

During an annual inspection carried out by CB1 on 27.6.2017, the use of non-organic untreated seeds without prior-derogation was detected. On 17.7.2017, the CB notified the operator that the affected harvest of 2017 must not be sold as organic. This was followed up by the CB during the next inspection. The audit team noted that this measure had little effect on the operator as the harvest in question derived from parcels which were still in either the first or the second year of conversion and in any case would not have been eligible to be sold as organic. Nevertheless, the CB downgraded two of the parcels in conversion year two to conversion year one. All other parcels concerned remained in the status of conversion year one. No other measure was taken against the operator. CB1 notified the above major irregularity to the MARD on 21.7.2017, together with a number of other major irregularities (i.e. declassification of land and products) dating back to January, May, June and July 2017. This is not in line with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 requiring an immediate notification of such cases.

An operator (medium risk) was sampled by CB2 during an annual inspection conducted on 17-19.6.2017. The laboratory results (30.6.2017) indicated the presence of Cyproconazole (0.032 mg/kg) and Axoxystrobing (0.015 mg/kg), both fungicides used in wheat production. The CB temporarily suspended the parcel affected and a counter sample was tested (in agreement with the operator) which confirmed the presence of the residue. On 31.7.2017, the CB informed the operator about the decision to downgrade the 2017 harvest of wheat as well as the field affected to conversion year one. The CB blocked the operator's account for the issuing of transaction certificate for organic wheat in the CB's own transparency-check tool. The MARD was only notified of this irregularity on 2.8.2017. The CB's operator list was updated accordingly, i.e. indicating a conversion period from 19.6.2017 to 19.6.2019 for the plot in question. The audit team noted that, despite this severe irregularity, the operator could continue to sell other produce (flax seed) as organic. The CB stated that, according to the catalogue of measures the operator is decertified, i.e. expelled from the system after three such irregularities. The CB also stated that such a situation has never occurred so far. The MARD stated that, following their own audit, one operator has been expelled from the system in the past. The above mentioned operator stopped all organic production in June 2018 following which the entire account of the operator was blocked in the CB's transparency-check database.

CB2 noted parallel production of wheat during an inspection (16.5.2018) at an operator. The MARD was only notified of this severe non-compliance three months later on 9.8.2018, contrary to Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. The CB stated that accreditation standards require the confirmation of detected non-compliances to be confirmed by the CB Certification Council before they are notified to the MARD and that operators concerned must be given the opportunity to appeal. 11 Conclusions on Measures in cases of Irregularities and Infringements
There is clear evidence that CBs do not report major non-compliances in a timely manner to MARD and other CBs.

Operators continue to be non-compliant in particular in relation to parallel production and application for derogations which is indicative that sanctions are not sufficiently dissuasive. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS. The CA has made considerable progress in implementing official controls for organic production and labelling of organic products since the first Commission audit in 2013. There are however still some serious weaknesses. Although there is annual supervision by the CA and reports are comprehensive with clear deadlines for the rectification of shortcomings, the number of witness and review audits is low in relation to the number of operators controlled by CBs in Romania. There is a risk that the CA is not furnished with sufficient information to thoroughly assess the CBs performance of official controls in the organic sector. The CBs' risk analysis do not always guarantee that all high risk operators are identified and hence controlled with the appropriate frequency. For example, a major irregularity by an operator in a year does not necessarily lead to an increased control frequency of the operator in question in the following year. CBs are overly focussed on controlling the organic activities of operators and have a tendency to overlook the significance of the operators' non-organic activities. Such an approach also leads to a bias in the risk assessment. Operators were sanctioned in line with the CBs enforcement procedures and in response to major non-compliances such as parallel production of annual crops. Yet such sanctions had little impact on the operators' behaviour. This situation may be due to the fact that, in Romania, many organic operators are entities with large non-organic and a much smaller organic activity. The economic impact of product decertification is low in such circumstances. In addition, operators were rarely suspended. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 19 October 2018 with representatives from the CAs. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The representatives of the CAs offered some initial comments and provisionally accepted the findings. 12 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The CAs are invited to provide details of the action taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion (action plan), aimed at addressing the recommendation set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report.
