recommendations.text: To take targeted action to enforce compliance with Union animal identification and registration rules and national biosecurity requirements within the non-commercial pig sector, focusing particularly on holdings located in high risk areas that engage in commercial activities outside their immediate localities · Article 17 of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU · Article 6 of Commission Implementing Decision 2013/764/EU · Articles 4(1) and 5(1)a of Directive 2008/71/EC · Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Recommendation based on conclusion: 72 Associated findings: 3, 6, 67, 68, 69, 70

citations.text: The veterinary authorities carried out a preliminary study in 18 counties at highest risk of ASF introduction to assess the impact and feasibility of implementing the new biosecurity rules. Key findings and conclusions reported include: a. A lack of awareness of the new biosecurity requirements among pig keepers, particularly on non-commercial holdings that have infrequent contact with veterinarians; b. Unregistered movements of live pigs between non-commercial holdings without notifying the authorised free practice veterinarian; c. Practical difficulties for veterinary inspectors to distinguish non-commercial holdings that engage in local trading activities from those that keep pigs solely for personal use; d. Many commercial farms in the 'medium farm size' group did not have the required biosecurity programmes in place; e. Compliance with biosecurity requirements on some industrial commercial farms was not satisfactory; f. The targeted enforcement of the biosecurity rules on commercial holdings (type A and industrial) is feasible. This may not be the case for non-commercial holdings.
Prior to the introduction of the new biosecurity rules referred to above (paragraph 1), biosecurity controls on non-commercial holdings were not performed.

According to information provided by the veterinary authorities, approximately 47% of the total pig population (approximately 4.3 million head) are kept by non-commercial keepers on 630 000 holdings. Most of these keepers own less than five pigs, which are kept for personal consumption. However, there is no legal limit and significantly larger numbers of animals may also be kept.

To illustrate this, ADNS reports indicate that at least 1 095 ASF outbreaks occurred on non-commercial holdings between June and November. The vast majority of these outbreaks occurred in holdings keeping one or two pigs. However, 136 outbreaks occurred on non-commercial holdings keeping between 21 and 100 pigs and 15 outbreaks occurred on non-commercial holdings keeping more than 100 pigs.

High levels of non-compliance with Union pig identification, registration and movement notification requirements on non-commercial holdings have been reported in several Commission audit reports. Most recently, mission report DG(SANCO) 2014-7045 included a specific recommendation4 on the subject.

The veterinary authorities have not taken appropriate actions to enforce the legal requirements nor to apply proportionate and dissuasive sanctions in cases of non- compliance, as required by Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 respectively.

The absence of reliable data on the location and movement of pigs within the non- commercial sector means that it is often not possible to trace animals that could have carried ASF virus to or from outbreak holdings. It also means that it is not possible for the veterinary authorities to enforce the prohibition to dispatch live pigs originating from the areas included in the Part III territory in the case of non-commercial holdings.

recommendations.text: To actively seek and pursue live animals, their products, persons and vehicles that may have carried ASF virus to or from the locality as part of the epidemiological inquiries conducted in cases of suspected or confirmed disease on small scale non-commercial holdings Article 8 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC Recommendation based on conclusion: 56 Associated findings: 43 & 44

citations.text: The operational manual provides instructions on the completion of the epidemiological inquiry: a. Detailed templates (Forms B.7 and B.8) should be used to prepare the initial and final epidemiological inquiry in the case of larger outbreaks (typically on holdings keeping more than 20 pigs). b. In the case of smaller outbreaks an abbreviated epidemiological report template (Form A.4) should be used. It collects contact details for the holding and records basic information about the farm collected during the initial interviews with the animal keeper and local free practice veterinarian.

The audit team reviewed the epidemiological inquiries carried out for several outbreaks on non-commercial pig holdings. In no case did the veterinary authorities trace the movement of persons, vehicles, pigs, carcases, semen, meat and other materials which could have carried the virus to or from the holdings in question, which is not in line with the requirement established in Article 8 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC.

The lack of thorough epidemiological inquiries on non-commercial holdings, which account for more than 90% of all ASF outbreaks, means that opportunities are missed to intercept infected live animals and contaminated products before they spread disease to previously uninfected areas.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the documents accompanying live pigs intended for slaughter, particularly those originating in the parts of Romania included in Part III of the annex to Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU, contain all necessary information to certify their eligibility for trade on the national and/or Union markets Article 5 of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU Recommendation based on conclusion: 75 Associated findings: 60, 61 & 62

citations.text: However, they do not specify the checks they should be made to verify compliance with the conditions (30 day residency, negative laboratory test results or regular holding inspections) that the live pigs must satisfy in order for their meat to be placed on the national market.

Furthermore, the service notes do not require official veterinarians responsible for holdings of origin to declare that these conditions have been verified in the documents that accompany the animals to the slaughterhouse. Consequently, official veterinarians responsible for applying health marks and/or certifying that the fresh meat has been produced from eligible animals are not in possession of all necessary information.

The audit team examined the documents that accompanied slaughtered pigs originating within the Part III territory. They had been completed in accordance with the service notes and did not include all necessary information concerning the eligibility of the animals.

Live pigs and their products coming from non-commercial holdings located in the areas defined in Part III of the annex to Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU are entering the national market. This has allowed the disease to spread long distances to counties that were previously free of disease. 5.5 COORDINATION Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, particularly Articles 4 ­ 10 Council Directive 2002/60/EC, particularly Annex VI (c) Findings

recommendations.text: To take all necessary measures to verify the operators' compliance with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000, as required by Article 22 of the said Regulatio based on conclusions: 32, 33 and 34. Associated findings: 19, 20, 22.c, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30.b and 31.

citations.text: In the commercial holdings visited, the audit team noted the following: a. The majority of adult bovine animals had two ear tags, some had one ear tag and, in one holding, only one animal was without both ear tags. This animal, however, had an electronic collar allowing linking of the animal with the holding register. Moreover, the holding operator had already in his possession ear tag duplicates also for this cow. b. With respect to young calves, in one of the holdings, all the young calves had ear tags while in another at least 10 (out of approximately 200 bovine animals) had not. The operator stated that the calves would be tagged soon (new ear tags were available at the holding) and demonstrated how to link the untagged calves to their mothers using the numbers from the calves' pens and records from the holding birth register. c. The commercial holdings' operators and private practice veterinarians notified newborn calves, movements from or to other locations and deaths of animals; however, in one of the two holdings visited, not all of the newborn animals were notified regularly and in a timely fashion. 6

In the backyard holdings visited, authorised veterinarians met by the audit team were responsible for ear tagging of bovine animals and, if needed, on behalf of the animals' owners, for completing the relevant identification documents (animal passports and movement documents) and inserting data in SNIRA. The veterinarians met kept the stock of new ear tags and maintained identification documents. However, the audit team noted the following: a. Out of the five backyard holdings visited, only one had fully completed passports and a complete set of movement documents. In this case, the situation on the holding also matched up the information from SNIRA and both cows had ear tags. b. In another backyard holding, there were no animals even though SNIRA database indicated the presence of nine bovine animals. Seven passports were available and two were missing and no movement documents "to" and "from" the holding were available. Neither the family representative of the cattle owner (2) nor the authorised veterinarian providing services to this holding were aware of the location where the animals had been moved to. c. In two other backyard holdings, the owners stated that, on an annual basis, they slaughtered one to two animals for their own consumption. In one of these holdings, the information on a recently slaughtered animal had not yet been entered in SNIRA. On the other holding, the owner stated that he did not apply ear tags to animals that would be slaughtered for own consumption, and therefore did not register them at all. d. Another owner of one backyard holding had 67 bovine animals (kept in two herds). One of the herds comprised 28 bovine animals of different ages out of which 10 lacked both ear tags. The age of the non-identified animals varied between few months to three years. The owner could present only 38 passports for his 67 bovines. Most of these passports were issued just prior to the visit of the audit team. Information from SNIRA indicated that some of these animals still belonged to the previous owner. The holding owner explained that he had only recently purchased the animals and the transaction had not yet been entirely finalised. However, he could not present any other evidence (e.g., the purchase agreement) supporting the statement. The CSVFSD officials immediately undertook to investigate the situation. Situations recorded in points c) and d) above constitute non-compliances with Article 4a(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 of the European Parliament and of the Council, which requires the owner to identify the bovine animals within a maximum of 20 days. 5.2.2 Official controls

The CSVFSDs have contracts with authorised veterinarians who carry out controls on animal identification and holdings registration. On a monthly basis, each CSVFSD verifies the reports of these controls submitted by the authorised veterinarians. The verification concerns at least 10% of the holdings submitted to the identification actions. The audit team noted that: a. The controls by authorised veterinarians take place regularly, every year and cover at least 3% of holdings in the counties. b. The controls on animal identification and holding registration by authorised veterinarians have a form of an inventory check, cross-checking all animals present in a holding (including bovines) with the status quo report from SNIRA generated prior to the visit. c. The authorised veterinarians inserted in SNIRA information on mismatches between the SNIRA status quo report and situation found at holdings, e.g., absence of animals recorded in SNIRA or presence of animals not mentioned in the SNIRA report. However, the mismatches identified at holdings have not been investigated further. Lack of adequate follow-up of non-compliances is contrary to Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000. 5.2.3 Bovine passports

While SNIRA is operational and available to all relevant users, the data available therein is incomplete for backyard holdings (retaining over 90% of the bovine population) in relation to the sub-populations relevant for the BSE monitoring and as such does not support the BSE monitoring and eradication system.

Official controls on identification and registration of bovine animals (inventory checks) are carried out as planned and are able to detect non-compliances, which are subsequently recorded in SNIRA. However, the lack of regular follow-up of these non-compliances weakens the effectiveness of official controls and in turn does not result in any improvement of the reliability of the national database, in particular, with respect to the absence of recorded movements of animals and of notification of newborn calves. 10

There is an increasing trend in the number of notified dead animals, indicating growing awareness of this obligation amongst the bovine animal owners; nonetheless, the mortality rate is still just above the half of the lowest expected. 5.3 BSE MONITORING SYSTEM, LABORATORY NETWORK AND TESTING ARRANGEMENT

recommendations.text: To ensure that an adequate system is in place ensuring proper collection, identification, treatment and disposal of ABP in accordance with the requirements laid down in Articles 12, 13 and 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion: 92 Associated findings: 84 to 90

citations.text: In September 2018, the only operator providing throughout the country a service for collection and disposal of ABP (all categories including fallen animals) got bankrupt and ceased its activity. Since then, and up to the date of the audit, there are no ABP processing plants in Romania authorised for collecting and processing ABP of Category (7) Follow-up on this recommendation covered also implementation of corrective measures to recommendation 2011-8950-5 requesting SRM produced as a result of home slaughtering of bovine animals, to be collected, transported and disposed of in compliance with requirements set out in Article 8(1) and Annex V to Regulation (EC) 999/2001. 21 1 and fallen animals. This situation resulted in a serious disturbance in the disposal of ABP originating not only from the husbandry sector but also from other sectors, namely the meat production, processing sector and the retail. Table 13 (see Appendix) presents detailed situation as regards the establishments processing ABP in the country at the time of this audit (8).

Overall, the system of collection and disposal of ABP, including of the fallen bovine animals from backyard holdings, has deteriorated since the previous audit. Therefore, recommendation 2 of audit report DG(SANCO)/2011-8941 remains unaddressed. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS With regard to Romania's application for review of its BSE monitoring programme it is concluded that, despite some positive trends observed, there are yet no grounds to allow for received 180 days of transitional period to comply with the requirements. 24 the frequency of testing to be relaxed. On the implementation of corrective measures taken to address recommendations made in the previous audits, some progress in addressing the recommendations of the previous BSE audit has been made only recently (as of 2017), whilst the ABP collections system has significantly deteriorated, resulting in recommendations from both audits remaining unaddressed. Whilst the bovine identification and registration system is in place and official controls on identification are carried out regularly, the system lacks effectiveness due to the underreporting of events, mostly from backyard holdings (keeping 90% of the bovine population), the absence of regular follow-up on non-compliances identified and the lack of analysis of the available data. In consequence, despite steadily increasing trends in the number of tested samples and some improvement in the functioning of the laboratory network, a certain proportion of eligible bovine animals remains not sampled and, consequently, not tested. The only area covered by this audit, relevant for supporting Romania's application and where official controls have been satisfactorily implemented for the last six years and are effective, concerns the feed ban. The existing system for ABP controls, which lacks a sustainable mechanism for regular collection and disposal of ABP, is not able to ensure that the ABP (originating at backyard holdings as a result of home slaughter), including fallen animals, are effectively collected and disposed of. Moreover, the current situation raises serious doubts whether ABP from the meat and the retail sector are collected and disposed of as required. The official controls have been ineffective in verifying and enforcing operators' compliance with the relevant requirements in this regard. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 27 September 2019 with the representatives of the NSVFSA. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. Representatives from the competent authorities did not indicate any major disagreement with these. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. recommendations.text: The CCA should ensure that the equine animals that after 1 January 2016 have not been identified within the time limits set out in Article 12, Article 14 or Article 43(2): - have a duplicate identification document which, when the conditions laid down in Article 29(1)(b) Regulation (EU) 2015/262 are met, classifies the animal in Part II of Section II of the document as not intended for slaughter for human consumption [Article 29(2)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262] or suspends the status of equidae for slaughter for human consumption in accordance with Article 31 of the same Regulation, and enters the details of the document in the database 4. [Article 29(3) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262] or - have a replacement identification document, classifying the equine animal in Part II of Section II of the document as not intended for slaughter for human consumption and enters the details of the document in the database [Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262] Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 4 and 56. Associated findings Nos 2 and 50. The CCA should ensure that keepers of equine animals meet the obligations laid down in Regulation (EU) 2015/262 as required in Article 3(4) of the Regulation and, in particular, that when non-compliances are detected all the necessary measures are taken to ensure they meet their obligations as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 41 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. Recommendation based on conclusion No 22. Associated findings Nos 17 and 35. The CCA should ensure that official controls at holdings keeping equidae are carried out on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency in order to meet the requirements of Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; in particular, the risk categorization and type of control to be done should consider the risk associated with those holdings where the movement of animals destined for human consumption is freque based on conclusion No 30. Associated finding No. 25. The CCA should ensure that only eligible equine animals are accepted for slaughter for human consumption. In particular, they should: - not accept for slaughter horses irreversibly declared as not intended for human consumption [Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262]; - not accept for slaughter and take appropriate actions when: horses are not properly identified (e.g. with microchips not recorded in the passport) [Point 1, Chapter III, Section II, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004] and/or it discovers that the accompanying records, documentation or other information related to the horse do not correspond with the true situation on the holding of provenance or the true condition of the animals or aim deliberately to mislead the official veterinarian [Point 5, Chapter II, Section II, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004]. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 55 and 96. Associated findings Nos 49, 53, 67, 70, 79 and 81. The CCA should ensure that when horses eligible for slaughter for human consumption are treated with medicinal products, the owner, keeper and/or the veterinarian responsible of the treatment meet the obligations laid down in Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. In particular: - when substances essential for the treatments of equidae are administered the details of the treatment are properly registered by the veterinarian in the relevant part of the passport in accordance with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1950/2006 and Article 37(6) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262; - in case non-permitted treatments are administered, the veterinarian responsible excludes the animal from the food chain and this is recorded in the passport and database [Article 37(3), (4) or (5) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262]; Recommendation based on conclusion No 114. Associated findings Nos 110, 111 and 113.

citations.text: From a preliminary analysis of the above national rules the audit team noted: The requirements of Regulation (EU) 2015/262, applicable since 1 January 2016, were implemented from 14 August 2017 when Order No 248/79/2017 was enacted. According to the national legislation in place prior to 14 August 2017, the authorities could release only duplicate passports when the equines were identified after the deadline established in the Regulation. This situation was not in line with Article 32(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 which lays down the requirement on the issuing body to issue replacement passports, which exclude permanently the animal from the food chain, in case of late identification. Since 14 August 2017 all types of equine passports (including replacement ones) can and are issued. ANZ explained that it is not possible to substitute the duplicate passports, issued during the above reported period by replacement ones because the national rules: a) cannot be applied retroactively and b) do not allow for charging citizens twice for the same administrative procedure (these types of passports are subject to fees).

National legislation/instructions for implementing EU legislation concerning the areas covered by the audit are in place. However, due to the delay in implementing 3 Regulation (EU) 2015/262, horses that should have been permanently excluded from the food chain, were not. No procedures are currently envisaged by the CCA to replace duplicate passports by replacement ones, resulting in ineligible horses continuing to enter into the meat production chain for human consumption. 5.2 Competent Authorities Legal requirements Articles 4, 5 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 5.2.1 Competent authorities

The audit team noted that the information in SIIE is not up-to-date and/or reliable, mainly due to the delay in implementing the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 (see paragraph 2). ANZ stated that it is difficult to keep the database updated because the input should come from other actors (e.g. the owners/keepers, veterinarians) and if they do not notify changes in the status of the animals and/or record them in the database the SIIE cannot be updated. In fact, they know that some horses that, given their age, should be dead are still registered as alive in the system because the owners did not notify the death. An example was also mentioned of 23 horses that were slaughtered but were still alive in the database. ANZ explained that the slaughterhouse did not notify the slaughter of the animals and now, no further actions can be taken because the establishment was closed and nobody is in a position to provide this notification. Movement controls

The central database for equine identification contains all the information required under EU rules. However, the information it contains is not complete, not up-to-date and thus not entirely reliable. 5.4.2 Official tasks at establishment level (2) Organisation of official controls

audits.title: Animal Welfare Transport

recommendations.text: The competent authority should provide sufficient information and instructions for staff, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to carry out official controls at the port, including inspections carried out according to Articles 19, 20 and 21 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusions: 16, 32 and 33. Associated findings: 1, 2, 3, 7, 21, 23, 24 and 26.

citations.text: The documented procedure for the inspection of a livestock vessel prior to approval is substantially a checklist which is part of Order 16/2010. This checklist covers all points included under Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, with the exception of drainage systems (Point 5).

The documented procedure for the inspection of a livestock vessel prior to loading animals is substantially in the form of another checklist: As already described in report 2015/7425, this checklist includes instructions to calculate and record the minimum required quantities of water and feed and available stocking density on board the vessel in order to verify compliance with these three requirements (see also paragraph 27). This checklist was last modified after July 2018 in response to the follow-up action by the Commission's auditing services on a vessel which was seen during the audit to Slovenia to evaluate animal welfare during transport to non-EU countries (report DG(SANTE)2018-6449, hereafter "report 2018/6449"). That vessel had also operated through Romanian ports prior to the audit to Slovenia. As indicated in report 2018/6449, that vessel was deficient regarding several provisions of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. The Commission services had pointed out that the checklist used by the Romanian competent authorities did not include points on drainage, lighting, or alarm systems. This checklist now covers all points required by Article 20 and Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation with the exception of drainage systems. 3

There is no documentary guidance or instructions explaining how to verify compliance with specific technical requirements which are not of a veterinary nature, e.g. ventilation capacity, functioning of emergency systems, and water and drainage pumps.
ANSVSA is drafting a checklist for the inspection of vehicles arriving at the port. This document has not been finalised yet. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT

Port inspectors are aware of the official controls they are required to do, but the absence of any records for these checks and for any subsequent action that might have been taken does not make it possible to verify whether they were in fact performed, their quality or 5 effectiveness.

CSVFSD official veterinarians are responsible for inspecting and approving livestock vessels. Procedures require that the transporter applying for the approval of a vessel submits all "relevant documents": The official veterinarians were not sure what "relevant documents" they had to collect in order to verify compliance with each of the technical requirements of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. There is no guidance or pre- established list explaining what should be included in the "relevant documents". Only one of the application files reviewed by the audit team had supporting documents for all the technical requirements indicated in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. This vessel had previously been authorised to transport animals by a non-EU country which has similar animal welfare standards. 6 All application files had deck plans, and water and drainage circuit plans. The official veterinarians used the deck plans to calculate the maximum surface area available to load animals in each deck (Chapter VII of Annex I to the Regulation). Only one of the application files reviewed by the audit team included the certification of the ventilation capacity for the entire ventilation system. In one application file there was no accompanying documentation certifying the air exchanges supplied by the ventilation systems. In another application file this certification was provided for only two of the ventilation fans.

Procedures for the approval of livestock vessels do not explain how to verify compliance with the specific technical requirements of the vessel, in particular ventilation, drainage and watering systems: All approval records indicated that the vessel had been checked for, and complied with, the minimum air changes per hour of forced ventilation systems in each deck, as required by Point 2 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. There was however no documentation to support this decision. The official veterinarians could not explain how they calculated the ventilation capacity on each deck without this documentation. All approval records indicated that the vessel had been checked for, and complied with, the requirement of Point 4 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, namely that the freshwater system was capable of continuously supplying water to the animals on each deck and that alternative pumping equipment was available. In each file the supporting documentation available was plans of the water circuit. The official veterinarians however could not properly read these plans (one-way valves, backup generators) nor explain how the watering system was structured and how it worked. Although the approval checklist does not cover the requirements for drainage systems (see also paragraph 2), the official veterinarians indicated that they nonetheless carry out this check against Point 5 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, i.e. that the drainage system was of appropriate capacity to drain fluids from the pens, that wells or tanks from where sewage is discharged were equipped with pumps or ejectors and that alternative pumping equipment was available. However they could not properly read the plans of the drainage circuits (one-way valves, wells and tanks, pumps and backup pumps) nor explain how the drainage system was structured and how it worked. The official veterinarians acknowledged that they do not have the technical competence to verify most of these requirements. 7

Port inspectors inspect vessels prior to loading animals. Procedures for this control, to verify that the equipment referred to in Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation is in good working order, do not provide the port inspectors with guidance on how to physically carry out these controls (e.g. how to verify that drainage tanks from where sewage is discharged are functioning properly).

All pre-loading checklists seen by the audit team indicated that the vessels inspected complied with the requirements of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, with the exception of the missing check for drainage systems (see also paragraph 1). The port inspectors were however unable to explain how they verify that certain systems and the relevant equipment (forced ventilation systems, drainage systems and pumps, alarms, back-up generators, etc.) are in good working order.

The insufficient information and instructions for port inspectors together with the absence of suitably qualified staff for assessing technical requirements for livestock vessels translates into a poor evaluation of technical requirements (such as air changes per hour on each deck of a livestock vessel, and the equipment used for watering and drainage systems on board a livestock vessel) during the approval and inspection before 8 loading. Therefore, official controls do no contribute to minimise the animal welfare risk linked to facilities and equipment.

Procedures include the relevant legal requirements but do not provide instructions for CSVFSD official veterinarians and port inspectors on how to verify these requirements as part of a practical inspection of a livestock vessel. Inspections of livestock vessels are therefore dependant on the experience of the inspectors, but not all requirements are adequately verified, which could have major implications for animal welfare during sea journeys.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take measures to ensure that reports of the official controls carried out at the port: on incoming vehicles and accompanying journey logs for the purposes of Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005; and for the purposes of Article 21(1)(a),(b) and (c), in particular that the animals are fit to continue their journey; are drawn up and their results properly recorded, as required by Articles 9(1) and 9(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. citations.text: ANSVSA is drafting a checklist for the inspection of vehicles arriving at the port. This document has not been finalised yet. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT

ANSVSA indicated that port inspectors check all livestock vehicles arriving at the ports but those checks are not being recorded. This is not in compliance with the requirements of Article 9(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

For vehicles which travel long road journeys before reaching the port, checks on journey logs include checks that a livestock vessel and a transporter for the sea journey have been identified. The port inspectors indicated that these are generally absent for those few journeys starting in Hungary (only 13 consignments in 2018). Although they are aware of these non-compliances, the port inspectors did not reported any non-compliance to their national contact point for informing the departing authority. Instead, they reported the results of the checks as 'satisfactory' in Traces.

Port inspectors are aware of the official controls they are required to do, but the absence of any records for these checks and for any subsequent action that might have been taken does not make it possible to verify whether they were in fact performed, their quality or 5 effectiveness.

The fact that deficiencies that port inspectors declare they detect are not recorded in Traces, nor transmitted to the national contact point, results in systematic unreported non- compliances to the Member State of departure concerned which, consequently, cannot take the necessary action to correct these issues.

citations.text: The Order of NSVFSA No 111/2008 of 16 December 2008 lays down rules for the registration of food businesses engaged in direct sale to final consumers, and supply of foodstuffs of animal origin and non-animal origin to other retail establishments. This Order was not notified to the Commission and Member States, contrary to what is required by Directive (EU) 2015/1535 of the European Parliament and of the Council. It lays down some relevant requirements: a. Article 2 defines direct supply of "small quantities" of raw milk to final consumers or other retail operators as up to 300 l/day for raw cow milk and up to 100 l/day for raw milk originating from other species; b. Article 7 permits the sale of that raw milk at events throughout the national territory; 3 c. Article 17 allows the direct sale of cheese up to 1 500 kg/week and of pasteurised milk/liquid dairy products up to 3 000 kg/week: types of dairy products shall be limited to a maximum of five (Annex I of this Order); d. Articles 3 and 18 establish that food business operators (FBOs) engaged in direct sale or supply of limited quantities to other retail businesses of raw milk or dairy products must be registered with the Cartography, Approval, Registration and IT Evidence Office at county level; e. Article 22 prescribes that such products must bear an identification marking of rectangular shape, bearing the words "produced in retail unit of type....", followed by the letters "VA" (meaning "retail"), the county code and the veterinary health and food safety registration number. The CCA reiterated that this mark also ensures the consumer that the manufacturing operator had been under official control: this qualifies the mark as a health marking, which shape is not defined for use by registered food operators by the EU legislation. Raw milk used in manufacture must comply with all quality and safety parameters laid down in the relevant legislation.

The Order of NSVFSA No 34 of 14 April 2008 lays down veterinary health and food safety rules for granting derogations to establishments producing foodstuffs with traditional characteristics. The order has not been notified through TRIS despite the fact that this notification is required under EU legislation. Derogations are possible for some requirements of Regulations (EC) No 852/2004 and (EC) No 853/2004 concerning floors, walls, ceilings, doors-windows-other openings, and measures and methods for cleaning and disinfecting rooms-equipment-tools. The County Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Directorates (CSVFSDs) are responsible for granting such derogations, having such businesses registered in a special register: each business has to be registered with the letters PT ("traditional product") followed by a unique registration number. None of the approved establishments have been currently granted such derogations.

National rules (Orders Nos 168/2014, 111/2008 and 34/2008) had provided national derogations for use of non-compliant raw cow milk, for direct sale of foodstuffs and for manufacture of traditional products. There is a system of supervision in place, however it was not able to identify important shortcomings relating to non-compliances with EU legislation. This limits the CAs to improve the official control system. 6 5.2.2 Registration/approval of food establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Articles 10(2), 138(1), 138(2)(c)-(j), 138(3), 138(4) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. When reviewing the outcome of one of the official controls of a sprout-producing establishment, the audit team noted that no checks were performed regarding import certificates of seeds for sprouting that had been imported from third countries. The CCA stated that for mung beans produced in third countries, certificates accompanying the consignments to the sprouting establishments are not required by the inspectors. This is not in line with Regulation (EU) No 208/2013.

The CCA explained to the audit team that they provided clear instructions to the counties about checking the fitness of seeds for sprouting. However, one of the county inspectors explained to the audit team that he considered an organic certificate for seeds sufficient as evidence for the fitness of the seeds for sprouting. This was not in line with instructions of the CCA and Regulation (EU) No 208/2013.

One of the counties granted a derogation to one sprout producer from preliminary testing of batches of seeds for sprouting, based on Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Part B of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The derogation was granted on the basis of samples that consisted of a mix of seeds from different batches. Additionally, the CCA explained to the audit team that the FBO had not been following the required monthly frequency of tests of the final product even before they had been granted this derogation. The CCA provided written evidence during the audit that the derogation was withdrawn by the county authorities and a financial penalty was imposed to the FBO for not following legal obligations regarding microbiological risk reduction. 12

Official controls of sprouting establishments are not verifying compliance with all the relevant legal requirements. Shortcomings in relation to the verification of compliance with traceability, import certificates, own microbiological analyses (frequency) and granting an unjustified derogation regarding "preliminary tests of seeds for sprouting" weaken the official control system, which could result in contaminated product being placed on the market.

recommendations.text: To determine and apply the ideal frequency and timing for the rabies vaccination campaigns considering the results of updated risk assessment in line with 2015 EFSA Scientific opinion (Update on oral vaccination of foxes and raccoon dogs against rabies) and Commission guidelines to design an EU co-financed programme on eradication and control of rabies in wildlife (SANTE/10201/2015rev1). Articles 32(1)(a), 33 (2), 34(2)(a) and Section 2 (point 1(a) and (b)) of Chapter 1 in Part 1 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689. Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusions 36 and 38. Associated findings 2, 6 and 7.

citations.text: The central authority did not apply the programme in 2018, which had a negative effect on the progress of eradication. The national legislation on public procurement caused the authority to miss another spring vaccination campaign in 2021, with likely similar negative effect on the rabies eradication as in 2018 (See Table 1 in Annex 3). Therefore, it could not follow the recommendations of the 2015 EFSA report and the 2015 Commission guidelines advising vaccination continuation for at least two years after the last reported case of rabies. This is not line with Section 2 (point 1(a)) of Chapter 1 in Part 1 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

The spring campaigns in 2019 and 2020 started at the end of May or beginning of June and finished in July, when the outside temperature was higher. The regular late start and finish of spring campaigns were not in line with the 2015 Commission guidelines. 4

The central authority and contractor took some preventive actions to mitigate risk associated to high temperatures (e.g. reduce efficacy of the vaccine), in particular by adapting the vaccination plan and the daily vaccine distribution schedules prioritising distribution early in the morning and trying to avoid days where temperatures rose over 30ºC. But the authority had not verified their effectiveness, e.g. they had not monitored the virus titre of the vaccine baits after their distribution to confirm that their potency was not altered by the exposure to high temperatures for several days in the environment. This is not in line with Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and with Section 2 (point 1(b)) of Chapter 1 in Part 1 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

The absence of oral vaccination campaigns in 2018 had negative impact on rabies eradication, and resulted in a decrease of the wildlife population immunity and a higher risk of spread of the disease. Similar negative effect on the rabies eradication is likely to happen in 2021 due to the absence of campaign during the spring.

The official controls on vaccine quality, its storage conditions, and manual and aerial distribution provided timely verification that the vaccine quality met the contract specifications, and that vaccine distribution was in line with the approved vaccination plan. The late implementation of the spring campaigns increases the risk of reducing the vaccine efficacy after their distribution. The authority and contractor took some actions to mitigate this risk but they had not verified their effectiveness. 5.1 MONITORING, AWARENESS AND SURVEILLANCE Legal requirements 8 Articles 10 to 13, 15, 18, 24, 26, 27, 31(1), 32(1), 34, 46, 57, 72 to 75, 77 to 79, 81 and 257(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429; Articles 5 and 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; Articles 3 (points 1(a) and (b)(ii)), 4 (points 1(a) and b(i)), 6(1), 8, 9, 12 to 15, and 32 to 36 of, and Sections 1 and 2 of Chapter 1 in Part 1 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689. The principles and techniques for rabies detection and the monitoring of effectiveness of rabies vaccination in foxes are described in the overview report "Rabies eradication in the EU" (DG(SANTE)/2016-8980). Briefly, vaccine baits contain tetracycline as a marker substance. When a fox tastes the vaccine bait, the tetracycline leaves a permanent trace in teeth and bone. Hunted foxes are tested for tetracycline (bait uptake) to check if the vaccine bait distribution has reached the target population. In order to become vaccinated against rabies (develop protective antibodies), the fox needs to bite into the vaccine capsule in the bait and swallow the vaccine. If many foxes have been in contact with baits (i.e. show traces of tetracycline) but have no antibodies, this could indicate a problem with the quality of the vaccine. The age of each fox should be determined to evaluate the effectiveness of the most recent vaccination campaign. Findings 5.1.1 Monitoring of bait uptake and population immunity

The table above shows that the number of enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) tests carried out was lower than the tests carried out to detect the tetracycline marker, both in 2019 and in 2020. According to staff from the laboratory, this was mainly due to the inadequate quality of the samples received. When they detected that problem, laboratory staff took action to correct the situation (e.g. by providing additional training, or distributing training material to the dispatching county laboratories).

In 2019, the majority of counties sampled 4 or more animals /100 km2, therefore reaching their sampling targets. The percentage of the target reached varied between counties, ranging from 51.33% to 165.46 % (for the fluorescent antibody test (FAT) tests). Seven counties (out of 40) took less than 80 % of their targeted number of samples, with two counties presenting data well below their targets. Those counties sampled only two animals /100 km2 (just above 50% of their plans).

In 2020, the variation between the counties in the percentage of the target reached was similar to the one in the previous year, ranging from 48% to 153.09 % (for the FAT tests). 26 counties achieved their sampling targets. Nine counties reached less than 80 % of their planned number of samples, with four counties well below their targets (less than 60 %). One county, bordering Ukraine; i.e. with a high risk of rabies incursion from the adjacent infected area, was not able to reach 50 % of the planned sampling target (less than 2 animals /100 km2).

The audit team analysed data provided for 2019 and 2020 for some counties showing that there had been an uneven geographical distribution of the samples taken within their territories. Both aspects; i.e. some counties not analysing the necessary number of samples and the potentially biased sample taken only from some hunting grounds, can significantly reduce the representativeness and reliability of the results obtained from their analysis and the validity of the conclusions drawn up at county and national level on the levels of immunity reached.

The authority has access to estimates of the geographical distribution of the population of wild carnivores in Romania, including the yearly hunting quotas and the hunting bags obtained at the end of the season, broken down per species and for each hunting ground. The data (see Map 5 in Annex 3) show an increased density of the jackal population in the southern part of the country, even exceeding in some counties that of the fox population. However, the authority does not take into account the estimates of all population of wild carnivores to fine-tune the planning of the rabies monitoring activities; e.g. targeting the jackal population in the selected area to obtain a representative image of the vaccine uptake and of the levels of immunity reached in this species.

The authority designed the rabies monitoring activities in accordance with the approved rabies programme and with general obligations in that respect laid down in Articles 3(points 1(a)(iv) and (b)(ii)) and 4 (point 1(b)(i)) of Regulation (EU) 2020/689. However, they did not apply those activities as planned. This is not in line with the provisions of the rabies eradication programme, recommendations of the 2013 WHO report and of the 2015 Commission guidelines, and point 1(d), of Section 2 of Chapter 1 of Part I of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

Despite the activities mentioned above, the authorities still lack sufficient understanding of how different factors contribute to the weaknesses identified in some areas of the country, e.g. underperformance in monitoring vaccination effectiveness, low levels of 16 immunity in wildlife in certain counties and under-notification and investigation of suspect cases and indicator animals. They have not identified and shared good practices that resulted in the adequate application of those measures in some well performing counties.

The inadequate implementation of monitoring of vaccination effectiveness in some areas of the country, combined with the sub-optimal surveillance for rabies, do not allow the authority to detect promptly the potential issues in the rabies eradication, in particular in oral vaccination of wild carnivores. This hinders the authority's capability to identify quickly the areas of the country at a higher risk of rabies spread where they need to focus additional prevention, surveillance and control efforts.

The chart above illustrates that the number of found dead foxes tested to detect the presence of the rabies virus has gradually decreased since 2018, and sharply in particular in 2020. The authority explained this could be due to the restrictions imposed for African Swine Fever and to the COVID-19 pandemic, which limited considerably the access for the general public and even for hunters to forest areas, and thus, lowered the chances to find fox carcasses. The central authority acknowledged they had insufficient collaboration with road authorities and local councils to increase the number of the road killed animals sampled for rabies investigation.

Data per county on the number of wild carnivores notified and investigated as suspect cases or indicator animals (see Maps 1, 2 and 3 in Annex 3) indicates that: o In 2018 and 2019 a higher number of the investigated cases originated in counties from the North (areas with a high risk of cross-border spread of rabies from neighbouring countries) and South-West of the country. o In 2020, the number of investigated cases in the same area in the North of the country and in counties with a similar risk profile situated in the East decreased significantly. o When the authorities of some counties found rabies cases in wild foxes, they intensified the application of surveillance, in particular in wide areas around the place where the infected animal was found. That surveillance included a significant increase in the number of foxes hunted in those areas and tested to exclude the presence of rabies (not exactly suspect cases or indicator animals) and a modest increase in the number of foxes found dead investigated. Nevertheless, those measures helped the authorities to better tailor their response to the changing epidemiological situation.

Data on the application of surveillance for rabies in domestic species and the geographical location of the rabies cases detected both in wildlife and in domestic animals complement the epidemiological picture described in the previous point (see Tables 3 - 5, and Map 4 in Annex 3). The data indicates that: o There are several counties with a significantly lower number of cases investigated as part of that surveillance, both in wildlife and in domestic animals. o All rabies cases except one were confirmed in counties with a high risk of cross- border spread of rabies from neighbouring countries not free from rabies (Ukraine and Moldova). o The only exception was a rabies case in a non-vaccinated dog detected in a county in the central part of the country, which had not had any rabies case recently. Despite their efforts in recent years, the county authority had not succeeded to enhance surveillance for rabies in that county, which had investigated hardly any suspect case or indicator animal during that time.

The continuous decrease in the number of suspect cases and indicator animals investigated to exclude the presence of rabies, both in wildlife and in domestic animals, which is more evident in an important number of counties, implies insufficient compliance with general responsibilities on animal health and obligations on disease surveillance for operators, veterinarians and for the authorities, laid down in Articles 10 to 13, 15, 18, 24, 26, 27 and 32(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. That situation is not in line either with the provisions for eradication of rabies laid down in Articles 32(1)(b) and (c), 33 and 34(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2020/689, on the basic strategy for the eradication programme, its targeted population and the surveillance the authorities must conduct in that context. 5.1.3 Control measures in the event of suspicion and confirmation of rabies

Although there are well-tailored information campaigns to raise public awareness on the disease, there has been an obvious decrease in the reporting of suspect cases and indicator animals investigated to exclude the presence of rabies in the last two years. This prevents the authorities from having more accurate and up-to-date epidemiological information on the rabies incidence and its geographical distribution in wild carnivores in Romania. Consequently, they might not be able to apply the measures promptly and to adapt them to reduce the risk of spread of rabies.

The inadequate implementation of monitoring of vaccination effectiveness in some areas of the country, combined with the sub-optimal surveillance for rabies, do not allow the authority to detect promptly the potential issues in the rabies eradication, in particular in oral vaccination of wild carnivores. This hinders the authority's capability to identify quickly the areas of the country at a higher risk of rabies spread where they need to focus additional prevention, surveillance and control efforts.

citations.text: To evaluate whether relevant legal requirements and standards applicable to ASF have been implemented effectively;

The instructions define several factors that the authorities must take into account when determining the overall risk category of establishments. These include the size of the establishment; the quality of construction; the overall standard of biosecurity; the type of production; and compliance with veterinary and traceability requirements.

The frequency of official controls for each establishment is set according to its risk category: Risk category Inspection frequency Low 1 per year Medium 2 per year High 4 per year Most outbreaks occur 11. So far, the impact of this initiative has been limited. Indeed, most on low or medium risk of the outbreaks on commercial establishments during 2021 establishments occurred on premised in the low or medium risk categories. Out of the commercial establishments keeping more than 65 pigs, around 60 % are assigned a medium risk, and 20% a low or high risk respectively.

This may be because: a. The risk factors the veterinary authorities use are incomplete. For example, they do not take account of weak points in the biosecurity systems of many commercial establishments: i. commercial links with other establishments (with pigs moving regularly between them without quarantine or post-arrival testing); ii. the direct sale of live pigs to non-professional holdings; iii. close proximity to other commercial establishments. 7 A review of the outbreak files during the audit showed that each of these factors might have played a role in the introduction of disease. b. The risk categorisation is inconsistent. The audit team noted several cases where the authorities at county level overlooked risk factors and assigned a lower risk category than was justified. 13. Veterinary officials also confirmed that the purpose of the official controls is to evaluate compliance with the legal requirements. It was beyond their competence to oblige business operators to put in place more sophisticated biosecurity systems than those that are established in the law. Official controls focus 14. Another factor that may limit the effectiveness of official on compliance with biosecurity controls is their potential to disqualify commercial legal requirements operators from receiving disease compensation. The Government Decision that lays down the disease compensation rules (see finding 43) may exclude from compensation any pig establishment that does not comply with biosecurity rules, or that has been "found by the competent authorities to have infringed the legislation in force". Although the legal interpretation of the latter exclusion is uncertain, the central competent authorities indicated that these exclusions could explain why official veterinarians might be reluctant to identify breaches of biosecurity rules during official controls. They agreed that disqualification from compensation would not be a proportionate penalty in many cases of non-compliance, which is contrary to Article 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 8 7 EARLY DETECTION AND SURVEILLANCE The high level of ASF awareness among commercial operators, together with arrangements to test samples collected regularly on commercial establishments, ensures the early detection of the disease and is a strength. High level of disease Awareness awareness on commercial holdings 15. The Romanian competent authorities have run intensive information campaigns to raise the awareness of ASF among the public and professionals. citations.text: The CA provided the audit team with a copy of the documented procedures dated 2007, which were prepared by the NPA. This document outlines the general tasks and responsibilities necessary for the inspectors to carry out their plant health duties including templates of relevant forms for use by the operator and CA. The audit team 1 Link to national legislation https://www.madr.ro/protectia-plantelor-si-carantina-fitosanitara/legislatie- nationala-fitosanitar.html 4 noted that the guidelines are based on repealed EU plant health legislation and do not include guidance for the implementation of any of the provisions on plant passporting established by Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and its implementing acts. This is not in line with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA stated that an up-to-date version of this document is being prepared and will reflect the new requirements of the plant health and official controls legislation, however no draft was available.

The CA stated that they do not have control verification procedures in place to ensure consistency of the implementation of the system of plant passporting among the 41 CPOs. This is not in line with Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the control system related to plant passports

The structure, responsibilities and legal powers of the CA are defined in national legislation. However, the lack of up-to-date documented procedures and control verification procedures and staff training does not ensure that the system of plant passports is implemented in a consistent manner and in line with EU requirements. 5.2 REGISTRATION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS Legal requirements Articles 65 to 68 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Findings 5.2.1 Official registration

The CA stated that they apply Article 65(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, however they have not exempt operators on the grounds of trading `small quantities', which has not been defined in national legislation. Nevertheless, the CA specifically exclude garden centres and retail outlets that sell directly to the final consumer from registration without the application of `small quantity' criteria. Furthermore, the CA stated they understood that operators selling though distance contracts are not exempt from registration but were unable to register them due to a lack of resources. This is not fully in line with Article 65(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on the registration of professional operators

There is a system in place for the registration of professional operators as required by EU Regulations. However, Romania provides no guarantees that all operators selling through distance contracts are registered. This may result in the movement of plants without a valid plant passport within the EU. 5.3 AUTHORISATION AND SUPERVISION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS FOR ISSUING PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 89 to 92 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 1 to 4 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 Findings 5.3.1 Authorisation procedures

In Romania, there is only one authorised operator and 1 552 registered operators, which are defined by the CA as 804 producers, 503 importers and 245 exporters. The CA stated they issue the vast majority of plant passports (see paragraph 26). Furthermore, 6 the CA stated, there has been no initiative to encourage registered operators to become authorised. Thus, the competent authority have failed to embrace the concept of Article 84(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, and the guidance provided for in recital no. 45 of the same Regulation, has not been considered. Recital no. 45 states that plant passports should generally be issued by the authorised professional operator and gives rise to authorising them to issue plant passports under the supervision of the CA. This is currently not the case in Romania.

According to the CA, the NPA is the authority responsible for the authorising of professional operators. The procedure for authorisation consists of the professional operator sending an email to the NPA, followed by an inspection by the CPO. It was noted that there is no formal documented procedure established for the authorisation of professional operators.

The CA stated that compliance of authorised operators with Article 89(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 is verified without the assistance of formal work instructions. Furthermore, the CA does not verify the obligations of the authorised operator to identify and monitor the points of its production process, and the requirements concerning the movement of plants, plant products and other objects, as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The CA stated that it determines informally the extent to which professional operators fulfil the criteria, by way of regular day-to-day interaction with the operator (see paragraph 11, 14, 18, 19, 22, 23). In addition, the competent authority has not made available technical guidance on the criteria to be fulfilled in the examinations to professional operators possibly interested in applying for authorisation which is not in line with Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827.

The CA are required to carry out official controls on professional and authorised operators at least once per year in order to verify compliance with EU requirements. During the site visits, the audit team learnt that inspectors plan controls on operators based on the biology of the pest or around the growing season of the plant. During the site visits the inspector examined the crop closely for the presence of pests and recorded their findings on official inspection forms. Copies of these inspection reports were 2 https://www.anfdf.ro/sanatate/ghid/ghiduri.html 7 provided to the audit team (see also paragraph 23). In addition, the inspectors frequently visit operators upon request, to carry out official controls on new consignments when they arrive or when notified of the suspected presence of a pest. Many of these new consignments include regulated goods from other MS that are accompanied by a plant passport. Some of these operators were visited at least once a week. The CA stated that this is something they always did since before the new EU requirements came into force. The audit team observed that a risk assessment is not always applied to these controls. Data such as, species, type of plant produced, origin, growing cycles or history of compliance is not taken into account and therefore do not justify these increased level of checks as required by Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66. The option for reduced frequency controls as provided for in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66 is not applied in Romania.

As part of these controls the CA stated, they also carry out checks on compliance with the format of the plant passport. However, the CA did not identify plant passports which were not issued in accordance with Article 83 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 as provided for in Articles 1 and 2 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313. Issues such as the absence of a border line, the background colour being determined by the colour of the packaging, the absence of the EU flag, the word `plant passport' not placed where it should be. In some cases, the plant passport had the EU flag and word plant passport cut off, due to the potential issues with printer used etc (refer also to paragraph 28 and 29). Furthermore, it was noted by the audit team that the CA has not reported any plant passport non-compliances since the new EU plant passport Regulations came into force. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports
The CA has not fully embraced the concept of the new system of plant passporting with the objective of placing greater responsibility on professional operators.

In 2021 the border control post (BCP) issued 5 015 passports for imported goods coming from third countries. The audit team noted that majority of the formats of these 10 plant passports issued at the BCP mostly met the EU requirements, however there were some inconsistencies identified in the format of traceability code `C' used by two BCPs. Some BCPs were using the CHEDPP number and others were using their own in-house coding system. This is not fully in line with Article 4(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, where the CA should ensure consistency and effectiveness of official controls across its territory. 5.5.2 Issuance of plant passports by authorised operators

The authorised operator visited, printed the passports directly onto the trade unit under the supervision of the CA. According to the CA these passports are checked randomly but without formal work instructions. (Refer to paragraph 19 where the audit team identified issues). In the case of own produced plants, the packages were issued with the operator's own registration and traceability code and in the case of purchased seed a replacement passport was issued containing information pertaining to the original consignment. Registered operators are required to keep all plant passport records for at least three years. 5.5.3 Plant passports combined with certification labels

The audit team noted during a visit to a professional operator, the CA did not issue replacement plant passports for imported vegetable seeds being sold on in smaller lots than the original imported consignment to other professional operators. According to the operator a replacement plant passport wasn't necessary because the checks were already carried out at the BCP. It was evident during the visit that the operator did not understand the objective of the EU plant passport requirements. It was also noted at the time, the inspector did not disagree with the operator's comments. Although this was an isolated incident, it resulted in the movement of regulated goods without a plant passport, which is not in line with Article 79(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.5.5 Application of the exemptions provided for in EU law

The issuance of plant passports is generally in line with EU requirements with the exception of some isolated incidents, where there was misinterpretation of the EU plant passport requirements by both the CA and the operator. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF PLANTS AND PLANT PRODUCTS WITH PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 69, 79 to 83, 88 and 93 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Articles 1 to 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety Findings 5.6.1 Official controls on traceability

The CA stated that they do not carry out plant passport traceability checks on authorised professional operators, which is not in line with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see paragraph 23(c)). However, the operator visited demonstrated to the 12 audit team a functional traceability system for different lots using the operator's own professional IT platform in line with the requirements of Article 89(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 for authorised professional operators. 5.6.2 Official controls on sales through distance contracts

While traceability of regulated goods was demonstrated to the audit team by the authorised operator visited, it is not checked by the CA. Furthermore, checks on operators selling through distance contracts to the final consumer are largely excluded from official controls. This may result in the movement of plants without a plant passport or movement of plants without a plant passport linked to a traceability system, thus posing a risk to the integrity of the plant passport system in Romania. 5.7 ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS Legal requirements Articles 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Findings

The CA informed the audit team that there have been no non-compliances identified in the plant passport system during the audit period from 2020-2021. However, the absence of documented procedures gives no assurances that non-compliances can be dealt with in line with EU requirements (see paragraph 6 on documented procedures). Although requested during the audit meetings and by email, the competent authority did not provide a clear legal basis to take action in the event of a non-compliance with regards to plant passports. This is not in line with Articles 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 13 Conclusions on enforcement actions

The CA did not provide a clear legal basis to take enforcement action in the case of non-compliances with regard to EU plant passport requirements. This may result in the CA not having the legal powers to take action in the event of a non-compliance and without the appropriate guidance, therefore risking the spread of regulated pests into the EU. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Romania has a structure in place that provides a basis for the implementation of the EU requirements for the system of plant passporting which is led by a central authority and competent staff. However, the competent authority has not embraced the concept of the EU plant passport legislation, which confers responsibility for issuing plant passports to authorised operators. Instead, plant passports are mostly issued by inadequately trained inspectors who do not verify the knowledge of authorised operators or their examinations or carry out traceability checks, due to the lack of guidance on the relevant requirements. This is compounded by the absence of verification of procedures and the lack of knowledge of those selling through distance contracts. Although requested, the competent authority did not provide a clear legal basis to take action in the event of a non-compliance. The cumulative effect of these shortcomings results in the competent authority being unable to implement the EU requirements in a consistent and effective manner and do not give the level of assurances in their system as required by EU plant passport legislation. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 24 June 2022 in the form of a videoconference between the audit team and representatives of the NPPO, during which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit team were presented. The NPPO offered initial comments on the findings and conclusions presented by the audit team. 14 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The NPPO is requested to provide details of any actions taken or planned, including deadlines for their completion, aimed at addressing the recommendation set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this report. citations.text: In all establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP plan was deficient in all five establishments. In general, the hazard identification part of the operators' HACCP plans was inaccurate (several potential hazards were not identified/assessed) or very 4 generic without the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification (as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) and consequent risk assessment. This issue was not reflected in any of the inspection reports seen and operators were thus unaware that there was a deficiency. The audit team noted that during the interviews some inspectors correctly identified these deficiencies.

In two establishments visited, the FeBOs identified critical control points in their own hazard analysis. However, the audit team noted that the established monitoring/verification procedures were not adequate for these critical control points. Additionally, the corrective actions described in their own hazard analysis were very general and did not correspond to the implemented corrective actions. Based on the scrutiny of the records of previous official controls, these deficiencies were overlooked by the feed inspectors during previous inspections.

While the planning of inspections is largely based on appropriate risk-related factors and allows for official controls to be carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of the inspections, and thus of the overall official feed controls, is weakened by a number of shortcomings in inspectors' assessment of (i) feed business operators' hazard identifications within their hazard analyses and critical control point plans, (ii) operators' traceability systems (in particular collection and storage of retained samples), and (iii) operators' compliance with labelling requirements. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

citations.text: Routine inspections include verification of operators' traceability systems, including the operators' obligation to take samples of ingredients and from each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market, or of each specific portion of production (in the case of continuous production) in sufficient quantities, using a procedure pre-established by the manufacturer (hereinafter `retained samples'), as required in part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit team scrutinised operators' documentation on collection, packaging, labelling 5 and storage of retained samples, interviewed inspectors who usually control those establishments and made the following observations: · in one establishment, retained samples were not collected (and stored) from feed additives and premixtures used for production; · in two establishments, significant number of the retained samples were not adequately sealed; · in one establishment, the operator did not collect retained samples from "non-critical microelements" such as amino acids and vitamins; · in one establishment, retained samples from finished products were not collected at all. These observations are not in line with the legal requirements established in part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and were not identified in any of the recent inspection reports seen.

While the planning of inspections is largely based on appropriate risk-related factors and allows for official controls to be carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of the inspections, and thus of the overall official feed controls, is weakened by a number of shortcomings in inspectors' assessment of (i) feed business operators' hazard identifications within their hazard analyses and critical control point plans, (ii) operators' traceability systems (in particular collection and storage of retained samples), and (iii) operators' compliance with labelling requirements. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

citations.text: Verification that operators meet legislative labelling requirements forms part of routine inspections. At all of the FeBOs visited, the audit team scrutinised operators' labels and other relevant documents, interviewed inspectors who usually control those establishments and made the following observations: · In two feed material producers, accompanying documentation relating to bulk consignments did not mention that the products were "feed material", which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 15(a) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. In addition, there was no compulsory declarations (crude protein, crude fibre, starch and total sugar) related to the feed materials placed on the market, which is not in line with the requirements Article 16 (1b) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. · In one establishment, for compound feeds marketed in bulk, the accompanying document did not contain information on vitamins, microelements and amino acids used to produce these compound feeds. This is not in line with legal requirements of Article 11(2) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009 since several of these feed additives (e.g., vitamin A, vitamin D, zinc) have maximum limits for the targeted animal species. · In one label of complementary feed, the type of the feed was not correct which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 15(a) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. · In one label of complementary feed containing feed additives with established maximum limits, the label did not contain clear dosage instructions, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 17(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. · In one label of a complete feed containing coccidiostats, the label did not contain the exact concentration of the used coccidiostats but provided a range of concentrations (e.g., 40-50 mg/kg). It is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 15(f) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. Labelling-related deficiencies were not identified in any of the recent inspection reports seen. 6 Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
