citations.text: In the two laboratories visited, the audit team scrutinised validation documentation for eight analytical methods (e.g., determination of mycotoxins, heavy metals, pesticides/non-dioxin like polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), botanical impurities, etc.) and noted that a number of methods had not been validated for all matrices routinely tested by the laboratories: heavy metals method had been validated for compound feed only while diverse feed materials (including minerals) and feed additives were tested for; pesticides/PCBs method had been validated for wheat only although other feed materials (e.g., sunflower oil, minerals) and feed additives (e.g., lysine) were tested for. Moreover, aflatoxin B1 method had been validated at 10 and 20 ppb (laboratory dependent) while the maximum content for, inter alia, compound feed for dairy cattle is 5 ppb and such products were regularly tested by the laboratories. Such approaches significantly limit the applicability of the methods and not in line with the requirements of part 1(b) of Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 8

For the eight analytical methods referred to above, the audit team examined the internal and external quality control systems in place. The audit team noted that, for the aflatoxin B1 testing in compound feed for dairy cattle, the fortification level of the positive control samples was 10 and 20 ppb (laboratory dependent) while the maximum aflatoxin B1 content for compound feed for dairy cattle is 5 ppb thus the fortification level of positive control samples for that type of feed was above the level of interest. For the PCBs method, less relevant matrix (wheat) was routinely used as positive control samples while largely other, very different, matrices (e.g., minerals, compound feed) were tested within the official feed sampling programme. Such approaches do not allow for effective ongoing method performance verification.

Notwithstanding the risk-based approach adopted for the planning of official sampling and the fact that the laboratories used for testing are accredited and appropriately designated, significant shortcomings in the implementation of sampling and especially in testing of official feed samples (both in validation of analytical methods and in implementation of internal quality control), undermine the legal and technical validity of the samples and the reliability of decisions made on the basis of the results. Cumulatively, these shortcomings weaken the overall effectiveness of the official feed control system. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency that varies between once per week (during the harvesting season) to once per month (from October to April), which would be in line with Article 61(1) an (4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 if harvesting was officially allowed exclusively during part of the year. However, at the time of the audit, this frequency was not met. According to the information provided to the audit team, there were different factors that prevented the sampling plan to be fulfilled (e.g., availability of vessels and other logistic problems, rough weather conditions), or that undermined the usefulness of complying with these frequencies (i.e., the long turnaround of results currently provided by the biotoxins laboratory).

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency similar to the biotoxins; therefore, the same observations made above (paragraph 17) regarding required frequencies and the difficulties faced by counties CA are relevant here.

The classification of production areas would be consistent with the EU classification requirements if harvesting is officially allowed exclusively during the summer (harvesting period). If harvesting is allowed during the whole year, the absence of appropriate frequency for sampling does not allow the authorities to ensure the same level of health and safety guarantees for the mollusc harvested outside this period.

The current design of the monitoring programme for microbiological quality seems adequate for the harvesting period, but the programmes for the presence of biotoxins and phytoplankton are not fully aligned with EU requirements and are not fully implemented. This could compromise the ability of the competent authority to detect possible exceedances of biotoxins limits. The delays in obtaining laboratory test results lower the effectiveness of the monitoring.

recommendations.text: ensure that the official monitoring of production areas and the decisions following it comply with the requirement of Article 61 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Recommendation based on conclusion No 39. Associated findings Nos 17, 20, 21, 25 and 28.

citations.text: According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency that varies between once per week (during the harvesting season) to once per month (from October to April), which would be in line with Article 61(1) an (4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 if harvesting was officially allowed exclusively during part of the year. However, at the time of the audit, this frequency was not met. According to the information provided to the audit team, there were different factors that prevented the sampling plan to be fulfilled (e.g., availability of vessels and other logistic problems, rough weather conditions), or that undermined the usefulness of complying with these frequencies (i.e., the long turnaround of results currently provided by the biotoxins laboratory).

At the time of the audit, the location of sampling points for water coincided with the points for biotoxins. The competent authorities were considering the inclusion of a second sampling location per production area that would allow the early detection of changes in the composition of plankton containing toxins and the geographical distribution of this plankton that can suggest an accumulation of toxins in LBM flesh, as required in Article 61(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency similar to the biotoxins; therefore, the same observations made above (paragraph 17) regarding required frequencies and the difficulties faced by counties CA are relevant here.

According to the relevant procedure, the competent authority must temporary close production areas when monitoring results show E. coli most probable number exceeding 700 per 100 grammes of flesh and intravalvular liquid (it is important to note that all production areas in Romania are class A and at the time of the audit there were no purification centres in the country). This closure is in line with Article 62(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Based on the information provided to the audit team, this closure is only enforced when such situation occurs during the harvesting period. This approach would be acceptable if harvesting is officially allowed exclusively during this particular time of the year.

According to the relevant procedure, the competent authority should conduct intensive sampling when monitoring results surpass the thresholds established at national level 7 (see paragraph 23). This aligns with Articles 61(3)(a) and 61(7) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. However, the competent authority confirmed that they currently do not adhere to this procedure. They consider its effectiveness is limited value due to several reasons: the same sampling locations are used for water and LBM, there are no additional water sampling locations for early warning, the long turnarounds times for results established in national legislation, and delays from laboratories results for biotoxins and phytoplankton, etc.

The current design of the monitoring programme for microbiological quality seems adequate for the harvesting period, but the programmes for the presence of biotoxins and phytoplankton are not fully aligned with EU requirements and are not fully implemented. This could compromise the ability of the competent authority to detect possible exceedances of biotoxins limits. The delays in obtaining laboratory test results lower the effectiveness of the monitoring.

citations.text: In addition, the monitoring programme for biotoxins does not include marine gastropods, and there are no data that compare the rate of accumulation of biotoxins with the indicator species. recommendations.text: ensure the following in laboratories: · That national reference laboratories are only designated if they comply with the requirements of Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and that they comply with the responsibilities and tasks established in Article 101 of the same Regulation. · That official control laboratories are only designated if they comply with the requirements of Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, that they comply with the responsibilities established in Article 38 of the same Regulation, and that they are submitted to the audits mentioned in Article 39 of the same Regulation. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 60-61 and 62-65. Associated findings Nos 45-49, 52, 54-59.

citations.text: The competent authority has designated NRLs for E. coli and for biotoxins in LBM, as required in Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. However, at the time of the audit, the NRL for biotoxins did not meet certain legislative requirements (i.e., Article 100(2) and (3)(c)(e)). 10

The audit team showed evidence of the implementation of part of the tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 by the NRL for E. coli (e.g., participation in proficiency testing organised by the EURL, provision of training and support to official control laboratories); however, this laboratory has not been able to organise an inter-laboratory comparative testing or a proficiency test between official control laboratories (there are only a few of them in the country) (required in Article 101(1)(c) of the same Regulation).
At the time of the audit, the NRL for biotoxins was not in a position to comply with most of the responsibilities and tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The competent authorities have designated official control laboratories, as required in Article 37(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In particular, they have designated three laboratories for E. coli (two testing LBM from production areas and one testing final products from dispatch centres) and one for biotoxins. However, designations do not include all the details required by Article 37(3) and, in the case of biotoxins laboratory, it does not require to use testing methods in line with EU requirements (see paragraph 57). At the time of the audit the laboratory testing for phytoplankton had not yet been designated as it did not comply with part of the national requirements for designation.

With regard to supervision of the designated laboratories, the CCA, in collaboration with the NRL for E. coli, carries out audits of these laboratories at county level, as required in Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, although limited to the conditions described in the previous paragraph. However, the CCA informed the audit team that a similar type of supervision cannot be carried out over central level laboratories designated for official controls; therefore, audits required by Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are not performed over the biotoxins laboratory. 5.3.1 Laboratories for microbiology
These laboratories regularly participate in proficiency testing but they have never participated in a proficiency testing with LBM sample matrix. 11 5.3.2 Laboratory for phytoplankton
There are two analysts qualified for the identification and quantification of plankton species. Both were internally trained and have plans to participate in external training in 2024.

The laboratory consistently conducts internal quality controls, with every sample being analysed by the two analysts by default to ensure the accuracy and consistency of phytoplankton results. The laboratory has never participated in a proficiency testing, but it intends to participate in one in 2024.

At the time of the audit, the long turnarounds times established in national legislation, together with the length of the analysis in this laboratory, limited the value of this monitoring for the competent authorities. 5.3.3 Laboratories for biotoxins

The official control laboratory for PSP and ASP uses testing methods which validation has not been internationally recognised, therefore they do not meet the requirements of Chapters I(A) and (B) and II(A) and (B) of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627, respectively.

The laboratory for lipophilic toxins uses the EU reference method established in Chapter III(A) of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. It mostly follows the EU reference laboratory standard operational procedure with a few deviations (e.g., it does not include part of the certified reference materials, certain quality control criteria, recovery correction and matrix correction). It is accredited by the national accreditation body, as required in Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The laboratory has carried out an internal validation for mussel matrix, as this is the species routinely analysed in this laboratory. However, the validation was not carried out for all the relevant toxins compounds and the validation report had a few shortcomings (e.g., it does not include part of the certified reference materials, precision data are obtained with certified reference materials instead of with naturally contaminated samples, etc.). At the time of the audit, this laboratory was not able to detect all the relevant compounds of the lipophilic toxin group established in Chapter III(A)(a) and (c) of Annex V to 5 EN 15204: Water quality - Guidance standard on the enumeration of phytoplankton using inverted microscopy (Utermöhl technique). 12 Regulation (EU) 2019/627, which poses a risk of underestimation of this biotoxin if such an episode occurs. The laboratory has never participated in a proficiency testing organised by a recognised provider; therefore, it could not provide evidence of the correct performance of the method (the laboratory informed the audit team of its intention to participate in one in 2024). The audit team took note of an exercise prepared by the NRL for this official control laboratory to test an unidentified sample of a certified reference material.

According to the information provided to the audit team, biotoxins results are normally issued in 4-5 days; however, it most of the laboratory reports assessed, the reporting time was one week. Despite the fact this is within the deadline established in national legislation, this provides limited value to the competent authorities to adequately manage production areas, therefore it cannot be considered as a timely delivery of test results as required in Article 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on laboratories

Although NRLs for E. coli and biotoxins are designated, the fact that they do not always fulfil the conditions of EU legislation for this designation or that they do not carry out all the tasks and responsibilities prescribed can have an impact in the quality and consistency of the results delivered.

The designation of official control laboratories includes all relevant laboratories (except for phytoplankton). As these laboratories do not always fulfil all the conditions for their designation and the designation does not always include all the necessary details to ensure timely and quality provision of results, this can have a negative impact in the quality of official controls over LBM and affect their efficient and effective supervision.

The technical competence and capacity of the official control laboratories for E. coli and phytoplankton, their fitness for purpose and their generally adequate analytical methods, instils confidence in the reliability of their results. This supports the authorities in the monitoring of production areas, allowing them to make informed decisions to safeguard the safety of molluscs.

Despite the technical competence and capacity of the official control laboratory for biotoxins, the fact that the validation of ASP and PSP testing methods is not internationally recognised, makes the reliability and accuracy of the results produced questionable for these two biotoxins. In addition, the fact that the laboratory for lipophilic toxins cannot analyse a number of compounds of this group (although it uses the EU reference method, internally validated and accredited) raises concern about the risk of underestimation of this biotoxin.
The absence of participation of official control laboratories in proficiency testing prevent the authorities to demonstrate the reliability of their results.

The long turnarounds times established in national legislation, together with the laboratories delays in providing timely results, have a negative impact on the quality of 13 official controls. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Although the official system for controlling bivalve molluscs and marine gastropods was only established in 2019, the authorities at different levels show good understanding of legislative requirements, and willingness to solve the deficiencies and to improve the system. The control system in place generally aligns with EU provisions, but it is implemented in full only during the harvesting period. Therefore, it would be consistent with the EU requirements if harvesting is officially allowed exclusively during the summer (harvesting period); otherwise, year-round harvesting lacks sufficient sampling frequency, compromising safety guarantees for LBM. The monitoring programme for microbiological quality seems adequate for the harvesting period, but the programmes for the presence of biotoxins and phytoplankton fall short of full EU alignment and implementation. The delays in obtaining laboratory results further hinder the effectiveness of the monitoring. Laboratories, though generally competent, face designation issues. Absence of participation in proficiency testing raises result accuracy concerns. There is confidence regarding E. coli and phytoplankton results due to the use of adequate methods and procedures, aiding effective monitoring. However, regarding biotoxins, the use of alternative testing methods that do not comply with the relevant EU requirements raises serious concerns about the validity of the results. 7 CLOSING MEETING During the closing meeting held on 13 December 2023, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit to the competent authorities present in the meeting. The competent authority acknowledged these findings and preliminary conclusions presented by the audit team and showed their willingness to solve the deficiencies and to improve the system. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. audits.title: Authorisation and controls of marketing and use of Plant Protection Products

recommendations.text: To ensure that a comparative assessment is performed when evaluating a new application for authorisation of a PPP containing an active substance approved as candidate for substitution and that it is also performed regularly and at the latest at renewal or amendment of the authorisation of existing PPPs containing candidates for substitution, as laid down by Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion No 16 Associated finding No 13

citations.text: Based on statistics on PPPs provided by the NPA, 416 out of the 1 387 PPPs, currently authorised in Romania, contain active substances considered as candidates for 5 substitution. Representatives from NPA stated that, in general, when authorising or renewing the authorisations of PPPs containing such active substances, there were no alternatives. However, the audit team noted that a comparative assessment had not been carried out for any of these PPPs to demonstrate that other, safer alternatives were not available. This is not in line with Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Representatives from NPA provided a procedure describing criteria and responsibilities for carrying out comparative assessments, however, it was noted that this procedure is in a draft form and has not been approved yet. Emergency authorisations

The general process of PPP authorisation involves representatives from three authorities, is clearly defined, sufficiently transparent and, despite some resource limitations, is generally implemented in a way that ensures scientific evaluation while limiting significant delays. Nonetheless, despite a relatively high number of PPPs containing candidates for substitution authorised in Romania, the CAs have not carried out comparative assessments against alternatives with potentially safer active substances, contrary to EU requirements and the Farm to Fork Strategy to reduce the risk of PPPs.

responses.response: re regarding comparative assessment in Romania, in accordance with art. 50 of Regulation (EC) no. 1107/2009, regarding the evaluation of a new application for authorisation of a PPP containing an active substance approved as candidate for substitution or for the renewal of the authorization according to art. 43 of Regulation 1107/2009 of PPPs containing candidates for substitution, is in final stage and will be discussed and approved in the next CNOPPP meeting, until the end of 2024 . From the beginning of 2025, the comparative assessment procedure according to art. 50 of Regulation (EC) no. 1107/2009 will be approved and implemented in Romania.

recommendations.text: To ensure that emergency authorisations are granted in line with Article 53(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 as interpreted by the Court of Justice of the European Union in its judgment on 19 January 2023 (Case C-162/21). Recommendation based on conclusion No 17 Associated finding No 15

citations.text: On 3 August 2023, Romania granted three emergency authorisations under Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 for outdoor use of seeds treated with a PPP containing imidacloprid (a neonicotinoid), contrary to the judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union of 19 January 2023 in Case C-162/21 Pesticide Action Network Europe and Others which clarified that even in emergency situations Member States are not permitted to authorise the placing on the market of PPPs for seed treatment, or the placing on the market and use of seeds treated with those products, where the placing on the market and use of seeds treated with those products have been expressly prohibited by an implementing regulation.. These emergency authorisations were notified to the Commission on 26th September 2023. On 9 November 2023, the Commission informed Romania that these emergency authorisations were not compatible with Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 as interpreted by the Court and recommended not to grant further similar emergency authorisations. Despite this, representatives from the NPA confirmed to the audit team that three more emergency authorisations for the treatment and sowing of treated seeds were granted on 16 November 2023, two for the use of imidacloprid and one for thiamehoxam. These authorisations were not notified to the Commission, contrary to Article 53(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Conclusions on authorisation of plant protection products

Emergency authorisations for the outdoor use of certain PPPs containing neonicotinoids have been granted repeatedly in violation of EU legislation, as interpreted by the Court of Justice of the European Union, the most recent of which were not notified to the 6 Commission. This entails potentially serious risks for pollinators. 5.2. recommendations.text: To ensure that controls of PPP operators in the chain of marketing and use of PPPs are performed following a risk-based frequency as required by Articles 9(1) and 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 35 Associated finding No 33

citations.text: The audit team noted the following: - Apart from the need to consider previous non-compliances and, for CAP agricultural users inspected on behalf of APIA, also the size of the farm, there are no risk criteria established at central level to prioritise inspections of PPP operators. For example, the following criteria are not considered: in case of PPP users, the type of crop cultivated, the risk due to the presence of water surfaces or neighbouring protected/vulnerable areas, and the results of the water monitoring programmes or, in case of wholesalers and retailers, their size/complexity. This is not in line with Article 9(1) and 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. - Due to the national legal framework (see findings 28 and 29), with the exceptions of the inspections carried out in the framework of the FITOS programme and those carried out on non-CAP agricultural PPP users, all inspections of registered PPP operators are not only carried out with several days prior notice but are generally also done at the same predictable time each year (just before the date of renewal of? ). Inspections of CAP agricultural users are usually carried out with a two-week prior notice, although the memorandum of understanding (see finding 20) clarifies that the prior notice should be kept as short as possible and be no more than 14 days. This general and extensive use of prior notifications is not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on planning of official controls

However, the planning of inspections is very limited, and they are generally not risk- based. In addition, there is a general and extensive use of prior notifications of inspections to all registered PPP operators and to a significant number of agricultural users. These shortcomings undermine the general effectiveness of controls and may be 10 one of the reasons for the remarkably low rate of non-compliances identified during inspections (see conclusions 54 and 61). Delegation of certain tasks Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that samples of PPPs are analysed to determine the presence of unacceptable co-formulants as referred to Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and the content of impurities whose maximum content is established in the approval of relevant active substances, as referred to Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. Such controls are required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 42 Associated finding No 41

citations.text: These samples are analysed using a network of laboratories, part of the NPL, all accredited to ISO5 standard 17025/2018 and participating in inter-laboratory comparative tests of PPPs with other Member States. The analyses include the determination of the content of active substances and the chemical-physical properties of 5 The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) is an independent, non-governmental, international standard development organization composed of representatives from the national standards organizations of member countries. 11 PPPs. Nonetheless, the audit team noted that co-formulants and impurities in active substances are not included in the analyses and this is not in line with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Consequently, the CAs are unable to verify the absence of unacceptable co-formulants in PPPs, in violation of what stated in Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in its Annex IIII and cannot determine whether certain impurities do not exceed the maximum content permitted in the approval of the relevant active substances, as required by Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. Moreover, only around 25% of these analyses have the analytical method included in the scope of accreditation. Representatives from the NPL explained that they are working to obtain a flexible scope of accreditation. Conclusions on laboratories used for formulation analysis of plant protection products as part of official controls

NPL is the designated laboratory for PPP formulation analyses, and it is accredited to ISO 17025/2018. This provides some basis for ensuring reliable results of tests and analyses although this basis could be strengthened by extending the range of analyses included in the scope of accreditation. Moreover, not including analyses for unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities in the sampling programme undermines the overall capability of the controls system to ensure the safety of the PPPs placed on the market. 5.3. citations.text: Furthermore, the audit team noted the following: - at retail level, the sale of PPPs authorised for professional use is not restricted to persons holding a certificate of training, and official controls do not pay attention to that, contrary to Article 6(2) of Directive 2009/128/EC. Representatives from the 13 NPA stated that this is due to the difficulties in interpreting what constitutes `professional use' of a PPP in Romania and that their priority is to ensure that retailers undergo the required training and are included in the certification system as laid down by Article 5(2) of Directive 2009/128/EC. - At the re-packer visited the audit team noted that inspections are carried out at least once per year, but the scope of the inspections is limited to the verification of the labelling of the final products and does not include controls, for instance, of the purchase of PPPs and the re-packing activities as such. Representatives from the central division of the NPA confirmed that the same limited scope of inspection applies to all re-packers and manufacturers and explained that this is because Romania considers that this is all EU legislation on PPPs provides for. Therefore, national legislation is expected to be adopted by the end of the year, allowing NPA to carry out more comprehensive controls on PPP manufacturers and re-packers. The audit team noted that Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 provides sufficient legal basis for carrying out comprehensive controls at all relevant establishments. Controls on imports

citations.text: Staff is recruited through competitions at the CA's central level, which include a written examination and an interview. At least a bachelor's degree on forestry, biology, agriculture or similar subjects is required for inspectors to apply for these competitions. All civil servants are then required to keep themselves updated within their area of responsibility. Representatives from the central division of NPA explained that there are no planned trainings to keep inspectors' knowledge up to date, nor regular meetings with them, but inspectors are always advised to regularly access the NPA website where the minutes of the NCAPPP's meetings are uploaded and, in case of requests from CPOs, or special needs identified by the central division of the NPA, online meetings are arranged. Nonetheless, the audit team noted that no minutes of these meetings are generally drawn up and that certain important information was not available to some inspectors met (see finding 48).

During their controls inspectors make use of `pest.exp' database, designed to include the necessary information about the PPPs authorised in Romania. However, the audit team noted that the database did not contain all the information included in the relevant PPP authorisations, in particular, information on the risk mitigation measures (e.g. buffer zone) is neglected. This has an impact on the implementation of controls on the use of PPPs (see finding 60). Conclusions on the competent authorities for official controls

Inspectors have a higher education highly educated, have access to control procedures and a database of authorised PPPs when carrying out checks on the marketing and use of PPPs. Inspectors met were generally sufficiently knowledgeable. Nonetheless, two of them were not aware of recent restrictions on the use of PPPs containing sulfoxaflor or terbuthilazine and were therefore not able to enforce relevant provisions on label changes or withdrawal of the affected PPPs. One of the retailers visited was storing several packages of a PPP containing sulfoxaflor with an obsolete label, but this was not noted by the inspector. Representatives from the central division of NPA explained that when such restrictions were decided these were included in the minutes of the meetings which are uploaded in the NPA website, but this may have been overlooked by inspectors. Without such information, inspectors are not able to perform the effective and appropriate checks required in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The inspectors met were sufficiently experienced and qualified. Furthermore, by looking at digital maps of the farmer's fields available from APIA website, the audit team observed that, in case of plots bordering a watercourse, only a generic warning reminding of the obligation to respect a 3-metre buffer zone was included; the need to apply a wider buffer zone depending on the PPP was not mentioned. A relatively high number of inspections of PPP users are carried out, but they identify a very low number of non-compliances. Moreover, certain provisions applicable to PPPs requiring risk mitigation measures to protect water surfaces are not verified because they are generally not available to inspectors. This is a matter of concern, exacerbated by the fact that the results of the water monitoring framework are not considered as risk criteria to prioritise inspections of agricultural users of PPPs. 5.4. OVERALL CONCLUSION There is a generally structured process for PPP authorisation, but repeated emergency authorisations are being granted in Romania for the outdoor use of PPPs containing active substances belonging to the neonicotinoids family, in violation of EU legislation. Moreover, the competent authorities have, so far, been passive in searching for safer alternatives when authorising PPPs containing active substances which are candidates for substitution. These breaches of the EU legislation can pose serious risks for human health, pollinators and the environment. The authorities involved in official controls on the marketing and use of PPPs are clearly defined, there is some collaboration between them, a relatively high number of inspections are carried out and a large number of samples for formulation analyses are taken and analysed by accredited laboratories. These elements, together with further measures introduced through national legislation, provide a good basis for the system of official controls. Nonetheless, there are some weaknesses which should be addressed to fully comply with the applicable EU provisions and to improve the system's effectiveness, which currently is low as the remarkably low rate of non-compliances identified during inspections may also suggest. The main issues are: a) inspections of operators are generally not risk-based b) most inspections are announced and predictable c) the scope of inspections is insufficient in the cases of re-packers and manufacturers, d) inspectors are not sufficiently informed when important changes of PPP authorisations take place and the PPP database available to them is incomplete and e) the sampling programme for formulation analyses of PPPs does not include the determination of unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities. 7. citations.text: The audit team noted that no BCPs have been designated and listed for food contact materials, (i.e. category PNAO-NHC(other)), and that official controls on consignments of food contact materials entering the EU are instead performed at the importers' warehouses, which is not in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR.

The audit team found that facilities and equipment at the port BCPs Constana North and Constana South and the airport BCP Bucharest Henri Coand were generally compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of goods for which they had been designated. However, the loading and storage facilities for goods of animal and non-animal origin at these three BCPs, and the inspection facilities at the airport BCP Bucharest Henri Coand, were not maintained and thus not easy to clean and disinfect. This is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 and 64(3) of the OCR.

The audit team visited one control point used for identity and physical checks on consignments of non-animal origin. The audit team found that the control point was not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Article 53(1)(a) of the OCR. There were no clearly dedicated unloading, inspection and storage areas, there was no drainage in these areas, and the floors of these areas were poorly maintained and thus not easy to clean and disinfect. In addition, the inspection area did not have a supply of hot and cold running water and hand washing facilities and it was equipped with a table that was not easy to clean and disinfect. Conclusions on the compliance of border control posts with minimum requirements

The evaluated BCPs, except for a suspended BCP for animals, had the minimum facilities and equipment in place for the categories of animals and goods of animal origin for which they had been designated, but the three BCPs visited were not well maintained. In addition, the Romanian authorities perform official controls on consignments of food contact materials entering the EU without having designated BCPs for this category of goods. The control point visited does not comply with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of goods for which it has been designated. These shortcomings have the potential to reduce the overall effectiveness of the official control system. 5.4 FOLLOW ­ UP OF PREVIOUS RECOMMENDATIONS The table below summarises the status of follow-up of two recommendations made in reports DG(SANTE)2015-7664 and 2018-6320, which were which were evaluated as `in progress' or `action still required' at the time of the last General Follow-up Audit to Romania by DG SANTE (ref: 2023-7658) in November 2023. citations.text: The Romanian authorities made resolute efforts in recent years to increase among backyards' operators the levels of awareness about, and compliance with requirements on animal traceability. However, despite introducing new legislation and strengthening official controls on the matter, the inadequate powers available to officials to enforce those new provisions keep holding back progress in this area.

An undetermined, but still significant number of illegal movements in the backyards population, and the underreporting to the national database of other events from those establishments (e.g., on-site slaughter), have an uncertain impact on surveillance for ASF and keep impairing epidemiological investigations when the disease is suspected or confirmed.

When ASF outbreaks occur in backyards, authorities do not always take effective measures to mitigate the risk of local disease spread. recommendations.text: To ensure the coordinated implementation by all relevant authorities of the measures contained in the national action plan for wild boar that aim to control and reduce that animal population and, thereby, avoid the spread of ASF and ensure the 13 On the legal references pertinent for each recommendation, please see the text of the associated findings for the explanation of their specific relevance. prevention, containment, and eradication of the disease. · Article 56(1)(b) and (c) of the ASF regulatio based on conclusions no. 5 and 6, and associated findings no. 56 and 92

citations.text: Implementation of surveillance for ASF in wild boar varies significantly between counties, but it confronts since the 2021/22 hunting season increasing challenges to find and test dead animals, which became a rare event in many of them4. Besides, the reluctance of the competent authorities to enforce requirements on ASF surveillance in hunting grounds, and delays in approving new legal provisions to introduce economic incentives to encourage searching for and testing of wild boars, keep impairing early detection and control of the disease.

The national action plan and legal framework to manage wild boar populations for ASF control, alongside the natural impact of the disease, led to a steady population decline until spring 2023. However, disagreements with part of the hunting community in some areas of the country, resulting in weak compliance with and enforcement of hunting quotas, exacerbated by recent climatic and environmental challenges, contributed to reverse that trend. While many hunting grounds apply biosecurity measures effectively, inconsistencies in population management and limited enforcement of ASF control policies create uncertainty about long-term disease control.

audits.title: Meat preparations and meat products

recommendations.text: The CAs should have adequate arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls, as required by Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in order to comply with Article 18(a) of the same Regulation for those controls aimed at verifying that FBOs meet the obligations outlined in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and provide assurances that their procedures based on HACCP principles are adequate. Particular attention should be given to · hazard identification and assessment; · strategies necessary to effectively manage microbiological risks associated with RTE meat products; · additional training of official staff, in accordance with their needs, to carry out their control duties in establishments producing meat products and meat preparations; · verification of the effectiveness of official controls through staff supervision following the aforementioned traini based on conclusion Nos. 23 and 80. Associated findings Nos. 16, 50, 54 and 60.

citations.text: Despite the above procedures, and training arrangements, the audit team found gaps in the knowledge of a number of CA staff, especially in relation to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and also on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) principles. This failure to keep the knowledge of staff conducting official controls up to date is not in line with article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The appreciation of the risk level of some hazards, in particular in high-risk RTE production areas, had an impact on the effectiveness of official controls in those areas. See also findings 50, 54 and 60. 5.2.2 Supervision of CA staff and audits

Although a system to deliver instructions, information and training material to CA staff is in place, covering topics relevant to the sector audited, it is not effective to routinely cater adequately for training needs on specific subjects, in particular official controls on the production of RTE meat products with high risk of microbiological contamination. This weakness impacts the effectiveness of the official controls.

In three of the six establishments visited, the audit team found that, in areas where exposed RTE meat products were produced, handled and/ or stored, the OVs failed to identify some non-compliances, did not correctly assess the importance of non- compliances identified or did not take the necessary measures to ensure that the FBO tackled the root cause(s) of some issues which, as a result, recurred. For instance: In one establishment, producing high volume of sliced product able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, the following points, observed in the high-risk production area, were classed as minor by the OV: · Some condensation over the area feeding final product to the slicer used for RTE meat products. This posed a high risk of contamination of the final product as well to the slicer (potential contamination of next batches passing through the same production line); · Poor post-operational cleaning, especially in the slicer used for RTE meat products; · Damaged wall panels rendering them not easy to clean and disinfect. In another establishment, the barriers protecting the walls in the slicing room were allowing the concentration of organic material (leftovers of the production) as well as the pooling of disinfectant after the cleaning process. Both matters posed a risk of cross contamination (microbiological and chemical, respectively). In these establishments, after this high-risk production area, the sliced RTE meat products were not subjected to any further steps able to address or eliminate the hazard. In another establishment the audit team found some long-standing issues that the official controls had either not identified or the OV had not taken appropriate measures to ensure that the FBO remedied the non-compliance and prevented further occurrences. These issues created a risk of cross contamination to the exposed RTE meat product and included the following: 10 · Inadequate ventilation that resulted in the pooling of water from condensation in a chiller used to store exposed RTE meat product, some of which was placed in low racks very close to the floor; · Long-standing dirt in ventilation grills in the same chiller containing exposed RTE meat product; · Cross flows between raw and RTE meat products, as slicing and packaging of RTE meat products was carried out in the same area as a packaging line for meat preparations. This is not in line with Annex II, Chapter I, point 1 and 2 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. HACCP based procedures

However, during the on-site visits, the audit team identified some non-compliances that had not been identified or reported by the CA in some of the establishments, mainly: · Product flow diagrams incomplete or not reflecting reality in one of the establishments. · Some hazards not considered or inadequately assessed. For instance, in one of the establishments Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus had not been identified as hazards in the packing/ slicing area. · In one establishment, the critical limit of the critical control point `temperature of fresh liver at reception' was set at 60 C, above the legal requirement of 40 C as specified in Annex III, Section II, Chapter V, point 1(b) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Microbiological criteria

In two establishments visited producing RTE meat products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, it was noted that the CA accepted that samples from the processing area and equipment were preponderantly taken after cleaning and disinfection. The European Union Reference Laboratory on Listeria monocytogenes (EURL Lm) Guidelines on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes recommends that the sampling should be carried out during processing in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain. Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense of security.

Official controls are risk based, supported by instructions and checklists and there is evidence that, in general, they are effective in identifying relevant non-compliances, in particular those regarding maintenance and hygiene requirements. However, these controls are not sufficiently effective to identify and enforce correction of non- compliances in relation to high-risk RTE production areas and in relation to shortcomings in the FBOs' food safety management systems.

recommendations.text: In order to comply with Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, the CAs should improve the effectiveness of official controls aimed at verifying that FBOs fulfil their obligations, as specified in Articles 3(2), and 5(2) of the same regulation. In particular, the verification that the food safety criteria applicable throughout the shelf-life of the products can be met under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use and also verification that environmental sampling for Listeria monocytogenes is conducted correctly. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 82 and 83. Associated findings Nos. 60, 63, 64 and 65.

citations.text: In two establishments visited producing RTE meat products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, it was noted that the CA accepted that samples from the processing area and equipment were preponderantly taken after cleaning and disinfection. The European Union Reference Laboratory on Listeria monocytogenes (EURL Lm) Guidelines on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes recommends that the sampling should be carried out during processing in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain. Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense of security.

The audit team reviewed some of the shelf-life studies used to demonstrate the aforementioned point and found that the demonstrations for different products in one of the establishments visited were done on the basis of a single durability study per meat product. These products had pH and water activity characteristics that supported the growth of Listeria monocytogenes.

According to the EURL Lm technical guidance document on challenge tests and durability studies for assessing shelf-life of ready-to-eat foods related to Listeria monocytogenes, it is not recommended to implement durability studies to validate a shelf-life related to Listeria monocytogenes because of its low prevalence, its low contamination level and its heterogeneous distribution in the food. The guidance mentions in this regard that, in most cases, results will be obtained from samples not contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes making it impossible to conclude on its 12 evolution in the product.

It was also noted that the above shelf-life studies did not take into account the expected storage temperatures at final consumer level and had therefore not been carried out under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required in Article 3.1(b) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

Some of the shelf-life studies carried out by FBOs producing RTE meat products to demonstrate compliance with food safety criteria, and accepted by the CA, were not carried out in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. As a result, their validity to demonstrate that Listeria monocytogenes will not exceed the limit of 100 cfu/g throughout the shelf-life of the product could be called into question.

The ability of some FBO's own-controls to detect Listeria monocytogenes in environmental samples is weakened by the FBOs choice of the timing of sampling. This timing, which is accepted by the CA, can impact the ability of the FBO to identify the sources of persistent strains of Listeria monocytogenes and provide a false sense of security.

recommendations.text: To ensure effective controls and enforcement of EU requirements on establishments performing livestock assembly operations Relevant EU legislation: Articles 130(b) and 133 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 Recommendation based on conclusion No. 44 Associated findings Nos 23 to 29.

When assessing the significance of this surveillance, it is important to consider that: a. the categories of sheep and goats that are exported to third countries are quite specific in terms of their production and are not representative of many other categories of small ruminant establishments in Romania. b. The number of animals tested (50,000 heads) among the total number of animals exported (during 2024, 1,231,121 sheep were exported to third countries and 517,787 sheep were traded with EU Member States) provides a statistically low level of confidence that the disease would be detected in the exported animal cohort, if present.

In response, the veterinary authorities prepared a PPR surveillance plan. However, substantial funding would be required for its execution and Government approval to proceed had not been granted at the time of the audit. Conclusions on outbreak management

By relying on clinical surveillance and targeted testing of animals intended for export, the veterinary authorities can provide only limited assurance that PPR is no longer present in Romania. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The veterinary authorities in Romania responded promptly and effectively to the PPR epizootic. Notable strengths in the system include the extensive veterinary clinical surveillance network, the quality of epidemiological investigations, the support of the laboratory network and close cooperation with other parts of Government at central and regional levels. However, without systematic serological surveillance, persistent disease circulation cannot be excluded. Significant shortcomings in the structure and operation of assembly establishments, coupled with weaknesses in official control of assembly operations, creates opportunities for the reintroduction and rapid spread of this disease and others. In addition, inconsistencies between the numbers of animals born, identified and removed from the national identification and registration system undermine its reliability for disease tracing purposes. 7 CLOSING MEETING During the closing meeting with the veterinary authorities, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. During this meeting, the competent authority provided all additional information requested by the audit team. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The Commission invites the competent authorities to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion (`action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below.
